#8929. 5 Signs You’ve Graduated From Beginner Cyclist Status

“When did you first realize you weren’t a beginner anymore?”

It’s a question I posed to my coworkers at Bicycling, many of whom have been riding and racing for multiple decades, at elite levels, across staggering distances, possibly uphill both ways in the snow.

I expected my inbox to be flooded with inspiring anecdotes; tales of triumph and woe; or at the very least, smug hot takes on when it’s OK to start caring about insider stuff like embro and VO2 Max.

But such was not the case. “Oh, I still feel like a beginner almost every day,” was the almost universal, almost completely BS response.

While I admired the humility, based on how many times my colleagues have teased me about my sock height alone, I knew all that self-effacement was completely false. So I pushed back, and eventually they coughed up a few earnest responses.

In many ways, they’re right—it’s great to never lose that wide-eyed rookie sense of discovery and fun. But it’s also pretty cool to see those little glimpses of progress along the way.

If you’re anything like us, here’s how you might have guessed you were starting to get a handle on this whole bicycle-riding thing, no matter how much chain grease might be stamped across your calves.

#8928. This Seated Twist Stretches Your Spine, Engages Your Core, and Enhances Your Awareness

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about a seated twist first appeared in the March-April 1994 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

To encourage new perceptual skills in my students, I like to ask them from time to time to practice in a new spot in the yoga studio. If you’re like most people, after a few classes you find yourself regularly gravitating to the same location, often within a few inches of accuracy.

The mere suggestion to place your mat in the front of the room instead of the cozy corner may make you decidedly un-comfortable. Changing positions enables you to see yourself and the world from a different vantage point, much as a photographer might circle a subject to get pictures from different angles.

It’s not surprising, considering the propensity of our species to form habits, that we tend to perceive our bodies from one perspective, including some aspects of ourselves while leaving others out.

Thus our perception of our body may become like a two-dimensional sketch, deprived of the volume, form, and texture that would extend our awareness into the three-dimensional realm. While Eastern cultures have investigated and honored the inner layers of the body as the key to our physical, mental, and spiritual health, most Western cultures have concerned themselves primarily with the body’s superficial layers. Because of this bias, most of us have come to view our movements as entirely dictated by the muscles and bones, unconsciously deleting other systems from our awareness. Keeping the mind on the outer layers, we become unable to feel or act from our deeper selves.

One of the body systems that brings us most succinctly into a deeper sense of self are the organs, the contents of the musculoskeletal container. Awareness of the organs gives our movements volume, form, and a sense of ripe fullness. Through the health and vitality of the organs, the outer layers gain their strength and form.

Just as we might bring our attention to the sensation of a muscle stretching, we can bring our attention to the sensation of an internal organ. When we change the vantage point of our awareness to bring the inner body into the foreground (an inner adjustment analogous to moving to a different place in the yoga studio), the way we experience ourselves and the quality of our movement will be quite different.

For most of recorded history, yogis have been engaged in just this kind of research, exploring the effects that the asanas (as well as pranayama and meditation) have on the deeper, subtler bodily systems. The ancient practitioners noted which movements and practices stimulated, purified, sedated, or neutralized the energy currents moving deep within the body, correlating these phenomena to health, longevity, and the elevation of consciousness. By contrast, they were not terribly interested in the state of their hamstring muscles, and traditional texts make few references to such structures.

Movements that twist the body compress, elongate, and massage the inner organs. Unfortunately, twists are often practiced exclusively from the perspective of the musculoskeletal system; we use the strength of the muscles and the leverage of the bones to force the body into rotation without ever inviting the soft inner contents along for the ride. Focusing on the internal organs not only reduces the possibility of injury, but stimulates and tones these deep structures by bringing our attention to them, just as electrical activity is created in our muscles simply by visualizing them flexing.

In this article, we’re going to look at how changing the vantage point of our awareness affects the practice of Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi (Marichyasana III), a seated twist.

Bringing attention to the inner body is a way to physically organize our presence on this center. Knowing that there is nowhere to “get to,” we can proceed with the full knowledge that we are on our way.

The following exercise was adapted from Sensing, Feeling, and Action by Bonnie Bainbridge Cohen. Sit on a cushion or blanket with your legs crossed. Close your eyes and let yourself settle. Bring your awareness to the soft inner contents of the torso surrounded by the musculoskeletal container. Imagine your body as two concentric cylinders with the soft internal organs on the inside and the harder musculoskeletal system surrounding them. Feel how the rise and fall of the breath swells from the core and communicates itself to the outer layer.

Now gently bring your awareness to each of your major organs. In the chest is the heart, slightly to the left of center, with the lungs on either side. In the upper left quadrant of the abdomen is the stomach; in the upper right quadrant of the belly is the liver, which extends up underneath the rib cage. The small intestines occupy most of the central and lower belly. In the lower right quadrant of the belly, the small intestine becomes the large intestine, which makes a hairpin turn to run up the right side of the belly (the ascending colon), across the top (the transverse colon), and down the left side (the descending colon), finishing as the sigmoid colon and rectum.

You may want to refer to an anatomy text for a more in-depth discussion of the internal organs. For now, sense their general position and volume, using your breath to palpate them. The kidneys lie on either side of the spine above the waist. The uterus is deep in the abdomen above the pubic bone.

Now bring your attention to your skeletal structure, as if you were seeing the body with X-ray vision. Extend your right arm over your head and bend to the left, focusing your attention on the bones moving. Repeat this to the other side.

Returning to the first side, initiate the side bend from the skeleton and then Shift your attention to the underlying organs, focusing on elongating the organs on the right side of the body and compressing the organs on the left. Did you go further? How did the quality of the movement change as your focus shifted?

Now initiate the side bend as a movement that arises from the organs. Breathe into and elongate the organs on the right side of the body, letting the skeleton follow. How did this experience differ from the one in which you had your mind on the skeletal system alone?

The organs are the seat of our deepest emotions; we physically experience strong feelings as sensations in the viscera (for example, the butterflies of fear or the tight knot of anger). Therefore, many people find that when they initiate movement from the organ system, the movement seems to arise out of their deepest self—that is, there is not a dualistic sense that the mind is “doing something” to the body. By contrast, when you perceive the body as nothing but a skeleton, it may feel as though your mind is manipulating your body like a puppet on a string.

Now integrate this new awareness of your organs into a simple twisting posture.

Some preliminary suggestions may make your task easier. One of the obstacles to twisting freely is the inability to sit upright with the normal curves of the spinal column intact. When the legs are extended, this problem may be further exaggerated because the hamstrings may pull on the base of the pelvis, causing the back to round (Figure 1: Incorrect). In this position, you are actually sitting on the base of the spine rather than on the sitting bones, and the collapse of the outer body makes it difficult to breathe freely.

To make sitting—and therefore twisting—a little easier, this first variation calls for both legs to be folded. By deactivating the hamstrings, we allow the pelvis to move more freely into an upright position.

Sit cross-legged with the buttocks elevated on a blanket or cushion. Place the right leg so the shin is upright, with the sole of the right foot directly in front of the left ankle. Inhaling fully, allow the abdomen to expand freely. On your exhalation roll the abdomen to the right, guiding the abdomen back against the spine to encourage the twist. Bring your left elbow onto the outside of the right knee (Figure 2).

With each breath, allow the soft inner body to move circularly in the direction of the twist, very much as if you were doing a belly dance. Once the lower torso is turning freely to the right, direct the breath more fully into the right side of the chest. Expanding the right lung with the inhalation, encourage the thoracic spine to move in and up. As you exhale, release the left lung from the center of the chest out into the shoulder, allowing the muscles along the back of the body to follow the changing shape of the lung.

As this occurs, the shoulder blade and then the arm will move further around.

Replace the elbow against the knee as necessary. When you feel you have reached your limit, stay for a few more breaths, simply letting the inhalation and exhalation oscillate the body slightly to and fro. Release on an exhalation and then repeat on the other side.

Now extend both legs in front of you, placing a blanket underneath your buttocks if necessary to create an erect sitting position. Sit with your back one arm’s length from a wall. Bend your right knee, placing the heel of the right foot in line with the sitting bone of the right side of the pelvis. Extend downward through the length of the left leg, simultaneously pressing the right foot down into the floor. Feel how this groundedness through the bones rebounds up through the body as the energy flows through the soft organs and the bones to support the erect carriage of the torso. When you release the downward movement of the legs, notice how the spine sags and the whole torso wilts.

Sense how the movements of the muscles and bones affect the shape of the internal organs, and vice versa.

As you inhale, direct the breath into the mid and upper chest. With each exhalation, successively turn from the lowest part of the belly to the head. Bring your elbow onto the outside of the right knee and place your hand against the wall, making sure that you are far enough from the wall that the shoulder is not elevated toward the ears (Figure 3). Use your arm to lift and support the torso, but do not overpower the soft movements of the inner body by using the arm to forcefully turn the outer muscles. Instead of using the arm as a “dictator,” let your arm become a “guide.” In the same way, wait for the inner body to yield to the movement, then encourage it with the guiding arm.

Take a few more full breaths before releasing and repeating the movement on the second side.

In this exercise you will focus on the contents of the spine—the spinal cord—to bring deeper awareness to your movement. Begin by sitting in Staff Pose (Dandasana) with both legs extended. Bend the left knee and place the heel of the left foot in line with the sitting bone. Now place the left hand immediately behind the left buttock and use it to support the trunk.

Before beginning the twist, take a moment to bring a few central images to mind. Start by bringing your awareness to the contents of the skull. Sense whether the brain is balanced equally between the front and back of the skull. Exiting the brain is the brain stem; then the spinal cord runs through each vertebrae like thread running through a string of beads.

Think of your spinal cord as the tail of your brain and the vertebrae as individual beads, each with its own size and shape.

As you bring your awareness to the brain stem, notice how the spinal cord curves inward so that the cervical vertebrae stack up underneath the head. As you continue your mental journey down the back, the soft spinal cord curves outward, following the convex curve of the thoracic spine. As you move your attention down toward the base of the rib cage, the spinal cord loops back in and the five lumbar vertebrae stack directly under the center of the chest. Continue on down to the massive sacral bone which curves outward and articulates with the two wings of the pelvis.

Having established this anatomical map, begin to sense how the bones of the spine are positioned in relationship to the soft spinal cord. Are there any areas of the spinal cord that feel compressed, perhaps even red and sore from being pressed and rubbed by the bodies of the vertebrae? Are there vertebrae that feel as if they were glued together, or areas where the bones feel rotated or collapsed on one side? Use your breath to gently move your vertebrae as if you were rearranging very precious antique furniture in a room. Adjust the vertebrae so they glide over the spinal cord easily.

As you enter the twist, continue to gauge your movement to avoid any irritation to the spinal cord. (While the brain is insensitive to pain, the outer sheath of the spinal cord is richly supplied with sensory nerve fibers.) Imagine that you are initiating the movement from the level of the spinal cord. If you overpower the spine with the strength of the arm, the result will often be irritation in the spine during the twist and an ache in the back long after your practice is finished.

Once the torso has rotated so the chest is facing the left knee, you can take the “hand lock” by bringing the right arm around the outside of the left shin. Link the fingers or, if possible, hold the left wrist with the right hand. Exhale and draw the hands away from the shoulders, allowing the spine to lengthen strongly upward.

If taking the hand lock compresses the front of the abdomen and collapses the spine, you are moving your skeleton further than the organs can support. Be conscious of using your breath to shape the internal organs. Keep the front of the abdomen open and draw the base of the left rib cage in toward the waist to encourage full spinal extension. Turn the head to look back at the foot of the extended leg (Figure 4). Take a few more breaths and then release. Repeat on the other side.

To clarify the distinction between initiating movement from the inner body and dominating with the outer muscles, you might try the previous exercises again, this time exerting force with the outer body by using the arm as a strong lever. Notice the tone in the muscle tissue when you exert force from the outside, as opposed to the quality when you allow the inner body to give to the movement in its own time. Also notice how the two different ways of initiating movement create different psychological states.

Within each of us is a longing for wholeness. Like the spiraling shape of the twist, our spiritual path must constantly turn back toward the still center within us. The longing to “get somewhere” through yoga is a distortion of our true urge to return back to the undifferentiated, unchanging core from which all life expands.

#8927. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

#8926. Stop Chain Skipping: How to Adjust Your Rear Derailleur for Smoother, Cleaner Shifts

A step-by-step guide to cleaner shifts on mechanical and electronic rear derailleurs.

Many of us have been there—try to shift and the chain just does not want to get up into that next gear. That frustrating click click click as the chain can’t make the jump is like nails on a chalkboard.

The rear derailleur is a key piece of equipment on the bike—especially with the gaining popularity of single chainring setups. The good news is that adjusting a rear derailleur is a fairly straightforward process.

On bikes with cable-actuated derailleurs keep in mind that as you ride (especially after getting a new bike or a new rear derailleur cable installed) the rear derailleur cable will settle into the bike—you’ll hear shops call this cable stretch. Over time you’ll need to add a little cable tension to the system to make sure your shifting stays tight and crisp.

Below we’ll go through everything from how to do a quick cable tension adjustment to how to spot a bent derailleur hanger so you can keep your shifting smooth for your next ride.

Your rear derailleur moves your chain across cogs and maintains proper tension on the chain with every gear change. How? The chain runs around two jockey pulleys on the rear derailleur. When you shift to a larger chainring or cog, the shifter cable pulls the rear derailleur forward, causing the pulleys to push the chain onto the larger sprockets while keeping chain tension in check.

When you shift to a smaller cog, the shifter cable releases the rear derailleur, which swings outward, taking up chain slack and causing the pulleys to pull the chain onto a smaller sprocket. If everything is set up correctly, your rear derailleur should make one clean shift for every click of your shifter.

Before adjusting anything on the derailleur, first ensure that your rear derailleur hanger is straight. A bent hanger is often the cause of rear derailleur shifting woes.

The derailleur hanger is the part of the frame to which your rear derailleur mounts. Derailleur hangers are made to bend or break under impact and not destroy your expensive frame or drivetrain. On carbon and aluminum frames, this hanger is often replaceable. If bent inward, you can very gently align it. But your best remedy is to have your local shop use a special hanger alignment tool to fix it, or replace the hanger entirely. Universal derailleur hangers have gotten more popular, but different frames need different hangers. Pick up an extra hanger to keep at home, but make sure you have the right one for your bike. This small and relatively inexpensive part will come in handy when you need it in a pinch.

If your chain doesn’t move when you shift, or it skips cogs, your rear derailleur may be out of alignment. Hop off your bike and do this: Shift your chain into the biggest chainring and smallest cog, then loosen the cable clamp bolt (where the cable attaches to the derailleur).

Look for the high and low adjusters on the derailleur—often marked with an H and an L. Adjust the high-gear screw by turning it until the jockey pulleys line up with the smallest cog. Your chain should move smoothly around the cog and pulleys when you turn the pedals.

To check alignment with the largest cog, rotate the pedal forward and push the rear derailleur so that the chain shifts to the largest cog. If the pulleys take the chain beyond the largest cog, screw the low adjuster inward until this stops. Reattach the cable and tighten the clamp.

Fine-tune with the barrel adjuster, located where the cable housing enters the rear derailleur. For the best performance, position the guide pulley roughly 6 to 7 mm away from the cogs. If your chain skips when you shift to a lower gear, give the barrel adjuster a half-turn counterclockwise. (Tip: Think L for lower and for left turn.) A higher gear? Try a half-turn clockwise.

Sometimes the cause of a skipping-feeling of your shifting is a stiff chain link. This happens when one or more chain links doesn’t properly articulate, either from corrosion or damage to the chain. This can be mitigated by cleaning your chain and adding a few drops of lube to each of the rollers and pins. This creates a smooth and efficient chain and allows your rear derailleur to move through the cogs without hesitating. To check for a stiff link, gently backpedal the chain and pay attention to how the chain rolls off the derailleur pulleys. If any links skip, work some lube into the link and gently flex the link until the chain moves smoothly.

Also check your chain for excessive wear—an overly worn chain can also cause poor shifting. As a chain is ridden, the bushings and rollers in the chain wear out, causing slop to develop and the distance between the pin centers to increase. (This is commonly called “chain stretch,” though the metal in the chain hasn’t really stretched.) Generally, when a chain “stretches” by 0.5 percent, it is time to swap the chain.

The easiest way to test for wear is a chain checker tool. But you can also use a ruler. A fresh chain measures 12 inches from pin center to pin center. If it measures more than 12 ¹⁄₁₆ inches, change your chain.

After cleaning, add a few drops of lube to the pivot points. (there are eight) of the parallelogram linkage, cycle through a few shifts, then wipe off any excess lube. When you clean your chain, clear any muck from the inner and outer surfaces of both pulleys—it collects at the base of their teeth. Make sure to wipe away all the excess that may reside on your chain, pulleys, and pivot points.

First, remove the chain. Many chains use some sort of quick removal link to make this easy, so look for that first. If not, break your chain with a chain tool or, if your chain is joined by a connecting pin, by removing the pin (use a new pin to rejoin the chain). Loosen the cable-clamp bolt on the rear derailleur and pull the shifter cable out. Undo the hex bolt that attaches the derailleur hanger from the rear dropout.

Make sure your new derailleur is compatible with your bike’s shifters; eight- through 11-speed shifters must be matched with the same manufacturer’s equivalent derailleur. Attach the new derailleur to the hanger using its hex bolt. Reattach the cable and loop the chain through the jockey wheels before reconnecting the chain. Shift through all gear combinations to make sure everything is running smoothly. If it isn’t, turn the barrel adjuster on the derailleur in or out to fine-tune shifting.

While your electronic rear derailleur operates on the same principles as the mechanical version, the biggest difference is the electronic rear derailleur has a tiny motor doing the work of pushing and pulling rather than a cable. That motor is powered by a battery that sends and receives signals from either a wireless or wired connection to the rear derailleur.

With an electronic system, shifting is managed by firmware, so it shouldn’t go out of alignment once it’s set up—though it may be adjustable through an app or other software tool (and it may need firmware updates). If you’re having trouble with your electronic derailleur, first check to make sure the battery has enough charge. Make sure any cables are fully connected as well.

When electronic derailleurs are shifting poorly, one of the first things I check is the hardware. Bent derailleur cages, hangers, or damaged derailleurs can all cause poor shifting, so assess those parts while your firmware updates.

There are a few important steps to be aware of prior to adjusting or fixing your rear derailleur. Identify which brand of electronic drivetrain is on your bike. Each brand has a different procedure on how to troubleshoot or adjust your rear derailleur.

Once identified, confirm whether it is wired or wireless. Then, double-check that the battery or battery interface is connected or has power. The following steps are unique depending on which brand of drivetrain you have.

Step 1: Charge your battery and check the coin-cell batteries in the shift levers (as basic as this sounds, it’s often the issue when a SRAM AXS or Shimano Di2 drivetrain suddenly stops shifting).

Step 2: Download the manufacturer’s mobile app.

Step 3: Check for any derailleur or shifter firmware updates.

Step 4: Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for derailleur and shifting adjustment (often there are step-by-step instructions in the app or check the brand’s website for details).

#8925. 7 Knee-Strengthening Exercises That Prevent Pesky Knee Pain

Don’t let a twinge slow down your pedal stroke—or keep you out of the saddle.

Because cycling isn’t a high-impact sport, you’d be forgiven for thinking your knees are safe. But Tara Parsons, a USAC-certified cycling coach and Rapha Women’s Ambassador says she hears riders complaining about knee pain all the time. In fact, 23 percent of riders experience knee pain, according to a study of 116 professional cyclists—and you can bet that number is higher among amateurs.

The knee acts as a hinge between the hip and the ankle, so just think about how many times you flex and extend your knees during a ride. “If you’re missing 5 percent of your range or in a position that’s slightly less than ideal, a small issue can turn into a big problem for someone who's averaging 50,000 reps a weekend,” says Dane DeLozier, the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance in Boulder, CO.

“This, in combination with a lifestyle that involves sitting at desks all day, can cause the weakening of muscles of the trunk, such as the core, glutes, and hips,” adds Parsons.

From there, it’s a domino effect: “When those muscles become weak or underused, they can become inactive or underactive. And when that happens, the muscles that you use a lot on the bike, such as the quads, end up overcompensating. This overcompensation causes poor knee tracking and poor alignment throughout the pedal stroke, which can lead to knee pain,” says Parsons. And that’s not even considering the stress you’re putting on your knees if your bike isn’t fit correctly or if you’re positioning in the saddle is out of whack.

Pay attention to pain in the patellar tendon, the tendon right on the front of the knee, and the IT band, which goes from the hip down to the knee, says DeLozier—those are common areas for pain, irritation, and inflammation that can hamper knee movement. “If that irritation persists, it’s probably best to go see a PT or your physician to figure out what the root cause is,” he adds.

Whether you’re currently dealing with pain or not, it’s important to build up strength around the joint. Strength training off the bike is crucial to developing those muscles. Plus, “your weekly strengthening routine should involve not just strengthening and activation, but also foam rolling or other type of soft tissue manipulation and mobilization” to keep your muscles in peak condition, says Parsons.

Not sure where to start? These knee-strengthening exercises will help you pedal on pain-free.

How to do this knee-strengthening exercise: Perform 2 to 3 sets of each exercise two times per week. You will need a resistance band loop, a Bosu trainer, and a medium weight. An exercise mat is optional.

The exercises in this workout are demonstrated below by Noam Tamir, certified strength and conditioning specialist and founder of TS Fitness in New York City, so you can learn the proper form. Follow along in the video above with Brian Levine, USAT Level 1 coach and endurance athlete.

Place a resistance band loop around legs just above the knee. Lie on your left side with knees bent, and ankles, knees, and hips stacked. Rest your head on left hand to avoid straining your neck and rest right hand on mat in front of you. Keeping your heels together, rotate right knee up toward ceiling as much as possible. Return to starting position. Complete 15 reps, then repeat on right side.

Lie faceup on the mat with a resistance band loop around your legs just above the knees and knees bent, heels close to butt, arms at sides. Contract glutes, and press into heels to lift hips up toward ceiling so your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees as you simultaneously press knees out to keep them in line with hips and maintain tension on the band. Pause. Lower and repeat for 10 to 15 reps.

Start standing on a Bosu trainer with hands on hips for balance. Take a big step back with left foot and lower into a lunge with right leg forming a 90-degree angle. Press through right heel to return left leg to start. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on other leg.

Place a band around ankles and stand with feet hip-width apart so band is taut. Lower into a micro squat, then step out to the left. Bring right foot in so feet are hip-width apart again; continue walking, taking 15 steps to the left before reversing to take 15 steps to the right, keeping the band taut the entire time.

Start standing and holding a kettlebell or medium weight in right hand. Shift weight onto left leg and micro bend left knee. Hinge at the hips as you lower weight to floor and extend right leg back behind you for balance. Continue lowering the weight until you are about parallel to the floor while keeping back straight. Return to the starting position. Repeat for 10 to 15 reps then switch sides.

Start on all fours with wrists under shoulders, knees under hips, toes tucked, and back flat. While keeping knee bent, lift right heel up as if to “stamp” your footprint on the ceiling. Return to starting position. Complete 15 reps then repeat on left side.

Start on all fours with wrists under shoulders, knees under hips, toes tucked, and back flat. Extend right arm and left leg straight out until they’re parallel to the floor. Maintain a flat back, level hips, and focus on pulling your belly button toward your spine. Return to all fours, then raise left arm and right leg. Continue alternating for 90 seconds.

GIFs: Julia Hembree Smith; Video: David Monk, Joshua Wolff

#8924. Stop Mashing the Pedals: 6 Lower-Body Moves That Help Cyclists Ride Smoother and Stronger

Build balanced leg strength and a smoother pedal stroke with six cyclist-friendly moves.

Talented riders make cycling look easy. It’s true that we are all gifted with the natural ability of riders like Tadej Pogacar or Mathieu van der Poel. However, those riders didn’t get to where they are without dialing in the fundamentals.

The concept of mastering the fundamentals is a thread that runs through conversations with anyone associated with a team in the professional peloton. It can be easy to dismiss high-level riders as in a different league—in many ways they are. However, we can all improve on the basics, the fundamentals, that give a proper foundation to get faster from.

Improving consistency in your pedal stroke is a great place to start with these fundamentals. As a reformed pedal masher, I know this process all too well. I once received advice from a mentor in a bike shop who told me to think of my pedal stroke as a clock—try to target even pressure on each number around the circle. Admittedly I don’t take that approach every time, but the concept remains planted in the back of my mind as I start to mash up a hill.

Part of improving your pedal stroke comes down to improving any muscle imbalances you have in your legs, so it starts with training off the bike. Start to develop this strength as we roll into the winter. Many riders have their sights set on goals for 2027 while they bring their bikes into the local shop for the final tune-up of the year. Make this your first workout to get the season started on the right foot.

“Single-leg exercises can reduce muscle imbalances and strengthen weaker muscles,” says Nicole Simonin, a certified personal trainer. Incorporate these lower-body exercises to increase and balance out your cycling-specific strength.

How to use this list: Each of the exercises below is demonstrated by a certified personal trainer so you can master the proper form. Perform each move for the set number of reps with 30 seconds of rest between each exercise. Repeat the entire circuit 1 to 2 times for a complete lower-body workout, then add it to your routine 1 to 2 times per week.

Start standing in front of a low box or stair. Place left foot on the edge and let right foot hang free. Press through left forefoot to lift heel up, pause, then slowly lower. Perform 15 reps, then repeat on other leg.

Besides building strength and being in the right position on the bike, proper pedaling form also involves focused technique. “Incorporating the entire circle requires you to pull your foot back and up at the bottom of the stroke,” explains Simonin. “In the final up-stroke phase is a feeling of lifting your knee so you can incorporate your hip flexors. Using the circle technique allows you to not just rely on the quadriceps, but to also incorporate the hamstrings and hip flexors.” Basically, there should not be any room for wasted movement in your pedaling. Think of moving the pedals forward, down, back, and up. And keep these valuable tips in mind.

Among the best ways to achieve more fluidity in your pedal stroke are one-legged drills. One-legged pedaling forces you to pedal all the way through the stroke and develop your muscles accordingly. Whether you do this outside or inside on a trainer, try to make it a regular component of your off-season training. Start with 20 revolutions per side and increase to several minutes at a stretch. Repeat two to five times per ride for each leg.

Opt for a gearing that will help slow down the motion and really allow you to focus on your form. The idea is to eliminate the dead spot in your pedal stroke. Remember that you want to keep your toes relaxed at all times. Resist curling them up or clenching the sole of your shoe.

When on your bike, think about pulling your foot back and up as if you were scraping something off the bottom of your shoe. You should feel tension in your hamstrings, and when the pedal is lifting up, the feeling should be one of lifting your knee with an assist from your hip flexors.

Before you even start to practice pedaling circles, make sure your bike is set up correctly. “Your position on the bike is key,” says Jill Gass, a USAC-Level 1 Coach and certified skills instructor. “It is important to start with a proper professional bike fit that also looks at shoe and cleat setup. Proper bike position gives you the biomechanical foundation to improve your pedaling style and efficiency.” Specifically, proper cleat and seat height position mean the knee will be lined up correctly, and getting this trio dialed is how you can max out your power, says Gass.

If your saddle is too high, you’ll rock back and forth. If it’s too low, you’ll put undue stress on your knees. To determine proper saddle height, sit on your bike while leaning against a wall. Now drape both feet straight down. If your saddle height is set correctly, your heel should just graze the pedal when the crank arm is in the 6 o’clock position.

#8923. Veterans Who Turned to Yoga Are Now Teaching It—And Not Always in the Places You’d Expect

Veterans yoga has been in existence for decades, with several organizations providing free classes. But what has been changing is the number of veterans teaching yoga, both to their peers and the general public. Writer “Chez” Chesak explores how his former platoonmates and other former military personnel are introducing others to the practice.

When I was deployed to Iraq with the U.S. Army in 2005, me and the rest of my platoon were constantly jumping in and out of Humvees, ascending uneven stairs in buildings, climbing ladders in guard towers, and generally finding ourselves in constant motion—all with more than 80 pounds of armor, ammo, night vision goggles, and other combat load sitting on our shoulders. And then there was the tremendous and relentless emotional and psychological stress. Needless to say, we were all very wired and very, very tight.

One proactive and thoughtful soldier in our platoon, Jake Smith, suggested that yoga could probably help and offered to download some instructions and lead us through a class. For some reason—quite possibly to stay out of sight from other soldiers, who would have likely ridiculed us—we thought it best to climb onto the roof of our building in Kirkuk for an ad hoc yoga session. Jake, who was definitely not a certified instructor but certainly did his best, led us through various poses and we attempted to follow along.

Somewhere in between making shapes with my body and concentrating on my breath, it registered that there were dozens of buildings in plain view of our patrol base. And if we could see the surrounding buildings, anyone in those buildings could see us. Realizing that we could be in the sights of a sniper, we quickly wrapped up class and made our way back inside.

For most of us, it was our first attempt at yoga. Despite the fact the class was well-intentioned and received well, none of us continued practicing during our time overseas. Instead, we succumbed to more shoulder pain and mental duress.

But in the years since, some in my platoon—as well as active military personnel and veterans everywhere—have been getting past our initial biases against such a “hippy” activity and turning to yoga for an array of reasons, including support with lingering physical and mental health challenges. I’ve heard the quote “Yoga saved my life,” from numerous military veterans who expressed the sentiment with zero embellishment, exaggeration, or hyperbole.

With nearly 16 million veterans in the U.S., there are more who could benefit from yoga. A survey of 300,000 veterans and service members registered with the Wounded Warrior Project found that more than half of respondents struggled to manage their pain, with 95 percent experiencing pain in the previous three months and 76 percent acknowledging that pain interfered with their ability to enjoy life. Additionally, more than 50 percent experienced anxiety symptoms in the previous two weeks.

Many of the veterans who proselytize about yoga know firsthand its role in supporting individuals through the repercussions of surviving combat zones. Some proceed to take yoga teacher training and introduce others to the practice, sharing it every conceivable style and practice space, including studios, gyms, and corporate offices. And among them are also those helping fellow soldiers and veterans explore how yoga might help them navigate the complexities of PTSD.

Mike Cappel used to hate yoga. He served 12 years in Military Intelligence in the Army Reserve and three years as a Combat Engineer in the National Guard and readily admits his past loathing for the practice.

Thanks to doctor’s orders, he tried yoga, fell in love with it, and then took a summer class at the University of Cincinnati (U.C.). Cappel now teaches yoga to the Reserve Officers Training Corps cadets there, beginning with cadets who participated in his yoga warm-ups before the Army Combat Fitness Test (ACFT) swearing that they scored higher thanks to the practice.

“They all say they love it now,” says Cappel. “And I can see that they really do. We’ll have a whole battalion of people out there in the stadium first thing in the morning, all doing yoga.” The officers that run the program eventually decided to try his classes as well,and these days everyone does yoga together before taking the ACFT.

His yoga instruction isn’t limited to students in uniform. Cappel also teaches at the offices of corporate clients, local independent yoga studios, and chain gyms, and leads a total of 16 classes a week.

In contrast to exposing those new to the military to yoga, Chris Smith brings it to those who have come back from their tours of duty and struggle to reacclimate to everyday life. After serving as an Engineer in the Army for eight years and being deployed three times, including during the 2003 Iraq invasion, Chris separated from the military and from his wife. He was unhoused and struggling with substance abuse when he was committed to an involuntary five-day psychiatric hold at a hospital.

Eventually, Chris landed in a rental assistance program through Veteran Affairs (VA), used the GI Bill to get a degree from Marywood University, and then started a veteran resource center. In researching benefits, he learned about Warrior Strong, which provides free wellness services, including yoga, to veterans across 33 states.

Chris explains that after taking his first yoga class, he was hooked. He soon signed up for training to become an instructor. He and other Warrior Strong instructors currently deliver nearly 100 classes spanning yoga, fitness, meditation, and breathwork to veterans each month. The classes are conducted online as well as in-studio at the Scranton, Pennsylvania, location as well regional VA medical centers. He also volunteers his teaching time to a weekly breathwork class for the depression group at a local veterans center and a monthly meditation class at the drug and alcohol unit at a VA Medical Center.

“Yoga is what’s really helping me manage my PTSD symptoms,” says Chris. “It’s helped me reconnect with people because for a very long time I was isolating myself a lot. I credit it with helping me continue the journey that I started nine years ago.”

Other veterans take elements of how yoga best supports them and share it with a more generalized student population. Jessica Armendariz spent 21 years in the U.S. Army, serving in the Airborne, completing all four levels of the Amy’s Combatives hand-to-hand combat training, and deploying to Afghanistan. When she retired, her body was experiencing severe physical wear, joint pain, and elevated cortisol levels. She eventually found that practicing rigorous vinyasa yoga helped alleviate chronic pain and quiet her racing mind.

Armendariz currently teaches studio classes at Hot Asana in Southern Pines, North Carolina, and tries to share the same benefits with others. “I am trying to challenge you physically,” says Armendariz. “That’s not to say that the rest of the yoga goes out the window. Of course we do breathing, we do centering, and all those critical things, but for me, for it to work to feel authentic to me as a teacher, there has to be that challenge.” She also has training in yoga nidra as well as yin and restorative yoga.

Sometimes the adaptability of yoga and its built-in community become as much a part of the yoga experience as the poses. After Jeremy McMullen left the Navy, he became severely sedentary. That’s when his wife gifted him a yoga lesson. The retired Chief Petty Officer instantly found that it benefited his sleep as well as his physical and mental health. Now a yoga instructor, McMullen teaches in a studio, performs yoga on mountain passes during long-distance hikes, has led online classes, and teaches “beer yoga” at breweries, where the participants indulge in a beer or two together afterward.

McMullen sees a correlation between his role in the Navy and his role as an instructor. “The chiefs at work [in the Navy] are always trying to teach sailors the right way to do everything. I do the same thing as a yoga teacher, making sure to teach you your left and your right and your breathing and your mindfulness.”

Military veterans are no strangers to working in unexpected and remote places. Jared McKenzie, a medic in my platoon when we deployed, currently teaches yoga at studios, so it wasn’t entirely a surprise when he was inspired, during a recent multi-day whitewater rafting trip, to lead others through early morning stretches along the shore. He’ll be resuming his beach yoga classes on the outfitter’s 2027 River Soul Journeys whitewater rafting and yoga trip in Idaho.

McKenzie is looking forward to teaching yoga within the solitude and serenity of Idaho’s river canyons. “I love the juxtaposition of this trip where everyone will be blasting whitewater through the day and then slowing down in the evenings with riverside yoga and breathwork,” he says.

There are surely more vets out there who are just now trying a class and starting their own experience with yoga journey. Those who take the next step and become instructors can deploy out to studios and VA facilities, teach online, and maybe even lead a class in a river canyon or other backcountry location. And I choose to believe that none of them will be so foolish as to attempt a class on a rooftop in a combat zone.

Veterans interested in trying yoga will find free resources for veterans-focused, in-person and online classes and teacher trainings through the VA’s Whole Health program and various organizations, including Wounded Warrior Project, Veterans Yoga Project, and VEToga.

#8922. Want to Ride More at Home? These 9 Stationary Bikes Make Training Easy, Quiet, and More Consistent

Find the right at-home ride, whether you want a budget spin bike or a premium smart-bike setup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Weather and daylight don’t always cooperate with our riding schedules. And when we add work hours, family time, yardwork, and life’s daily grind, finding time to ride can feel impossible. Especially during the dark days of late autumn and winter, indoor riding becomes the only realistic option for many of us.

Luckily, indoor cycling is no longer the boring, arduous task it was only a decade ago. Today’s stationary bikes range from no-frills machines to fully connected setups. Some even feature live and on-demand classes, immersive virtual rides, and easy syncing with popular fitness platforms like Strava.

All of our editors and test team ride or train indoors for at least part of the year, sometimes even during the summer months to escape the heat. We’ve logged countless hours on stationary bikes and standard indoor trainers. In our testing, we’ve wrestled with finicky machines, endured glitchy interfaces and endless updates, and spent plenty of time grinding out virtual miles from our basements, garages, and home gyms; some of our editors have even taught spin classes.

Stationary bikes come in three main styles: Upright, recumbent, and dual-action. Upright models feel most like riding a traditional outdoor bike. Recumbent bikes offer a more reclined position, while dual-action bikes add upper-body work to the pedaling action.

Our testing and reviews focus on upright stationary bikes made by cycling-specific brands and general fitness companies. To differentiate between the two, we call models from fitness companies “exercise bikes” and those from cycling brands “indoor bikes” in this story.

Exercise bikes by fitness-oriented brands often feature a more upright riding position, multi-position handlebars with foam padding, and wide, comfort-style seats. The pedals usually have toe clips for use with running shoes.

Indoor bikes from traditional cycling brands typically mimic the body position, ride feel, and functional layout of outdoor bikes and feature dropbars, brake hoods, adjustable crank length, and narrow saddles. They usually feature high resistance for sprint workouts and virtual racing. These bikes used to be expensive, but prices have dropped over the last three years, making them a great choice for everyday indoor riders (not only hardcore enthusiasts).

The BowFlex C6 has the most capability at a reasonable price. High-quality and adjustable, this bike features Bluetooth connectivity so you can connect to apps like Peloton, Zwift, and Schwinn Trainer to join community rides and track progress.

The monitor displays time ridden, speed, mileage, heart rate, and resistance level. It doesn’t show wattage or precise RPM (it displays them on a scale). However, it does measure them, and you can see that data if you connect it to third-party training apps.

The flywheel is smooth and heavy, and you can crank the resistance up significantly through 100 incremental levels via a knob. Toe cages let you ride the C6 in regular running shoes or flip the pedals over and clip in with Shimano SPD cleats.

A great feature is the unit’s silence—you can use it day or night without waking your family. It comes with a forearm heart rate monitor and a pair of 3-pound dumbbells for light upper-body workouts while riding.

Want a more immersive experience? Check out BowFlex’s Velocore. It features a 22-inch integrated console with tons of class and entertainment streaming options, and is compatible with Zwift, Peloton, and JRNY.

If you don’t like traditional exercise bikes and want something that closely replicates the fit and feel of riding your actual bike, the Zwift Ride is an ideal solution—and the recently updated V2 model addresses issues our editors experienced with the first-gen model by adding adjustable crank length and saddle setback.

At its core, the Ride is an indoor cycling setup that eliminates the hassle of constantly mounting and unmounting your bike from a trainer or dedicating one bike solely for indoor use. The frame is exceptionally sturdy and has proven itself time and again under the stress of multiple test riders’ workouts. Paired with the reliable Kickr Core 2 trainer—our Best Overall smart trainer pick—the setup delivers a premium ride experience.

However, the real magic lies in its seamless integration with Zwift’s virtual world. You can join races, group rides, guided workouts, or explore immersive digital landscapes alongside fellow “Zwifters.” The most popular virtual cycling platform globally, Zwift succeeds by stripping away the monotony of indoor training. It gamifies the experience while offering social and competitive features that you can engage with as much—or as little—as you like.

The Schwinn IC4 is ideal if you want quick, easy access to ride metrics; you can see your data on the display—no subscription necessary. It also has a stand for your phone or tablet, USB charging for your devices, water bottle holders, and weights so everything you need is at your fingertips.

If you’re in the mood to be pumped up by a live class, Rouvy, or Zwift race, the Bluetooth option lets you jump right into third-party apps. The bike comes with a free two-month subscription to Schwinn’s platform, JRNY, which offers workout programming tailored to your preferences and over 200 virtual courses.

If you like the concept of the Zwift Ride but want an indoor bike with more adjustability and refinement, Wahoo’s Kickr Bike Shift is one of the best options. It’s essentially a stripped-down version of Wahoo’s super-premium, $4,000 Kickr Bike Pro; the Shift doesn’t include the Pro’s motor-electromagnetic resistance, gradient simulation, and some finishing details. While nifty features, they’re overkill for almost every indoor rider.

Like the Kickr Bike Pro, the Shift is quiet, super smooth, and easily adjustable to fit multiple users in a household. It also features standard bicycle component attachment. This makes it easy to replicate your outdoor bike’s fit on the Kickr Shift with your favorite saddle and handlebar. If you want the convenience and silence of an indoor bike, and a premium indoor riding setup, the Shift is the one to get.

Peloton redefined at-home fitness with its original bike—a sturdy, low-maintenance machine built to withstand years of sweaty daily rides. Its true draw, though, has always been Peloton’s vast library of on-demand and live classes, now spanning not only cycling but also running, core, and boot camp sessions. With the Peloton app, you can even take workouts on the go.

For years, the bike itself saw few changes—until the Bike+ arrived. It keeps the durable frame and quiet belt drive but adds a redesigned handlebar and a larger 23.8-inch touchscreen that rotates 360 degrees, making it easy to follow floor-based workouts. The model also features forward-facing Sonos-tuned speakers and auto-resistance that adjusts automatically to match instructor cues. Not everyone will use it, but those who do will love the convenience.

The most notable update is Peloton IQ: a built-in camera that tracks your movements, offers real-time feedback, and counts reps. There’s even a small fan above the screen for added comfort.

However, these upgrades come at a premium: the Bike+ is significantly more than the standard Peloton Bike. If you want to save $1,000, the standard Bike features solid build quality and full access to Peloton’s unmatched training ecosystem. But it doesn’t include auto-resistance, high-quality speakers, a rotating screen, Peloton IQ, a phone tray, and a fan.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike features a 35-pound flywheel and provides a smooth, quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable with a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches. Riders can also adjust the handlebar height and the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Although the Yosuda doesn’t connect to third-party sites, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned on the included single-button monitor. Below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame provides stability and durability, yet it’s easy to move thanks to the small wheels on the front edge.

If you’re spinning on a budget but want a connected experience, the Echelon EX-15 may be the stationary bike for you. This high-quality bike offers access to proprietary classes you can stream with an Echelon membership ($399.99 billed annually). Echelon’s membership isn’t limited to cycling content. The subscription offers rowing, running, strength training, yoga, and more. Enjoy workouts to music from artists including Pitbull and Lady Gaga—plus dance, EDM, hip hop, K-Pop, metal, Latin, and R&B.

The EX-15 bike itself is sized perfectly for smaller spaces, yet doesn’t skimp on comforts like an extra-large cushioned seat and padded handlebars. The mechanical knob lets you adjust resistance between 32 levels. You also get a free 30-day membership when you buy the EX-15 through Amazon.

It’s important to have one with solid construction and high weight capacity if you plan to put your stationary bike through the wringer. The Sunny Evolution Pro can withstand your most intense intervals and feels stable doing it. The 135-pound steel frame has a large footprint with leveling stabilizers in each corner to help prevent rocking.

Complementing that is a hefty 44-pound flywheel, which eliminates the inconsistent resistance you can feel near the top end of lighter wheels. The adjustable handlebar moves up and down and front to back, so you can dial in a position that's comfortable for your back, neck, and wrists.

The seat height accommodates riders with inseam lengths from 29 to 39 inches—a downside if you’re on the shorter side (Our 5-foot-2 barely made the cut, but awesome if you’re taller).

The Evolution Pro’s simplicity also makes it a great pick. Without Bluetooth connectivity (or even a monitor to display metrics), you can exercise without getting bogged down in numbers and be more in touch with your body at different PRE (perceived rate of exertion) levels.

The Keiser M3i is a studio-level spin bike with a clean, streamlined design and simplified interface. It has everything you need to nail your numbers in a hard workout, and then upload that data to apps like TrainingPeaks or Strava. The smooth flywheel is quiet, and its rear location means fewer sweat droplets land on it, so you can worry less about corrosion or wiping it down perfectly. The small monitor displays your power, cadence, time, gear, heart rate (if you’re wearing a connected strap), and total distance.

The media tray holds a phone or tablet above your handlebar so you can follow a route or guided workout as you ride, and it automatically uploads each effort in the included Keiser app to track your progress.

The saddle height adjustment uses preset stops; however, the wedge system lets you place the saddle in the precise spot you prefer. The looped handlebar is comfortable for a wide range of reaches, and the height adjustment accommodates riders as short as 4-foot-10 and as tall as 7 feet.

Stationary bikes come in three main options: upright, recumbent, and dual-action. The bikes recommended here are upright style, which puts you in a position that mimics how you’d sit on a traditional bicycle.

Recumbent exercise bikes seat you in a slightly reclined position with the pedals out in front of your hips rather than directly below, which can be easier on your back and neck. Dual-action exercise bikes have handlebars that move in and out, so riders incorporate their arms into the workout as they pedal.

Look for models with adjustable saddle height and position, plus adjustable handlebars. More adjustability makes it easier to find a comfortable riding position and get a good workout. Like a regular bicycle, a proper fit is crucial for the best experience. I like my indoor bike’s fit to match the position I ride outdoors.

All bikes feature bar-height adjustments, and some models let you adjust reach. Saddle height and setback adjustment options are also a must-have. They also have graduated markings, making it easier to get back to your preferred position after someone else uses the bike.

A dropbar offers hand positions that mimic road bikes, while a traditional bullhorn bar will be more familiar to those of you who frequent studio classes.

The two most common methods for regulating an indoor bike’s resistance are friction and magnets. Friction-based systems use leather or synthetic pads that press against a flywheel—It’s a simple, effective way to add precise, linear resistance. These resistance systems don’t require outside power to operate.

Magnetic resistance is quieter than friction systems. They use magnets (adjacent to the flywheel) to create an electric current that resists the wheel’s rotation. By increasing the current (strengthening the magnetic force), you have greater resistance. With no contact between the flywheel and magnets, this type of bike may offer a smoother ride than a friction-based one.

Some models use electromagnetic resistance controlled by software from a connected app. This allows platforms like Zwift to replicate hills and wind.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Bluetooth-equipped exercise bikes let you transmit your ride data directly to third-party training apps like Peloton or Zwift for in-ride metrics. If it has ANT+ capability, you can connect to extra sensors—like a cadence tracker or heart rate monitor—and display that data on your monitor or tablet. It’s not totally necessary for an interactive experience.

If you want to join virtual classes but aren’t sure which you’ll like (or you enjoy several), look for a bike with connectivity and media compatibility that lets you join the most platforms.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Most indoor bikes function similarly; the accessories that set them apart. The most basic models are as simple as it gets, just an ergometer with a weighted flywheel and a pad to set resistance. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes like the Peloton, with elaborate software for recorded and live classes.

Decide how much technology you actually need for your indoor rides. Some cyclists want a feature-rich experience with training plans, classes, and group rides, while others want a stripped-down bike that covers the bare essentials.

Measure your available space before buying. If you will need to move it, also check the model’s weight and whether it has wheels.

Seat comfort matters; if possible, test-ride the seat that comes with your stationary bike before buying to make sure it's comfortable for you. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.

Seat comfort matters. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
