#8921. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8919. COROS Doubled the Price of Its Bike Computer. Can the DURA 2 Compete With Premium Rivals?

COROS kept the feature that made the original stand out and rebuilt nearly everything around it. Now the DURA 2 has to justify its place among other premium options.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The original COROS DURA stood out for two reasons: battery life and price. At $249, it was a (relatively) affordable alternative to the Garmin and Wahoo computers most riders already knew. Just with a solar charging feature that made charging almost optional. But it also felt like the first-generation product that it was. The DURA 2 is COROS’s attempt to move beyond that niche and compete with computers from Garmin, Wahoo, and Hammerhead.

The DURA 2 has a new, unusually slim form factor, a larger 3.5-inch touchscreen, updated maps, and redesigned controls that replace the original’s thumb dial. It also adds voice commands, music controls, and a built-in bike bell. The screen is a memory-in-pixel display, rather than the bright, phone-like panel found on OLED displays on the Karoo and latest Garmin head units. COROS’s priority here is a legible readout while minimizing the power demand of the screen.

Battery life remains the headline. COROS rates the DURA 2 for up to 120 hours in standard GPS mode, or 70 hours with dual-frequency GPS, before factoring in solar charging. After 30 hours of riding with paired sensors, occasional navigation, and the screen at full brightness, my unit still had 77 percent battery remaining.

The price of the DURA 2 has changed along with the ambition. The computer costs $499 on its own, or $549 with COROS’s aluminum mount—a steep jump from the original, though you can skip the bundled mount if you already have a compatible one. The question is whether the DURA 2’s much longer battery life, improved interface, and the COROS ecosystem make it a compelling alternative at this price. After riding it, I think the new DURA is a much more complete and compelling computer. But it hasn’t quite closed the gap to its competitors.

The DURA 2’s memory-in-pixel screen won't win anyone over with vivid colors or smartphone-like detail. That’s fine with me. I don’t use a cycling computer to watch videos or scroll social media. I want to glance down, find the information I need, and get back to riding. The DURA 2 does that well, with arguably the most legible screen in direct sunlight I’ve seen.

The screen struggles most in inconsistent, high-contrast light, such as bright dappled sunlight through tree cover. This is when I wish the DURA 2 offered any kind of meaningful backlight. To my eyes, changing the screen brightness from full to all the way off made no noticeable difference. This wasn’t a huge issue on basic numerical data pages, which stayed very legible, but when you’re trying to discern map detail, it felt a little tough, especially while riding.

Some riders will still prefer the brighter, higher-resolution screens on the Hammerhead Karoo or Garmin’s high-end computers. That’s a valid preference. How beautiful a screen looks isn’t a huge priority for me.

The maps themselves are a big improvement over the original DURA. In my experience, the Hammerhead is still the standard for map legibility and ease of on-device navigation, but the DURA 2 is now quite good. It shows street names at closer zoom levels, and the map responds quickly when you pan or zoom. Both the processing speed and touchscreen response are dramatically better than on the first DURA, and are now close to what I expect from Garmin and Hammerhead.

One screen quirk is that Coros has no way to manually lock the screen. COROS says it will automatically lock when it detects too much rain. I would still like to have a manual lock setting, even if the automatic system works as promised. I suspect COROS could add that option in a future firmware update.

Good riddance to the dial. I gave the original DURA’s dial a fair chance, and it could be useful once I got used to it, especially with gloves. But I also found it clunky and a pain to use while riding. The DURA 2’s new haptic buttons work as advertised, and the touchscreen is far more responsive than it was on the original.

The screen is a little less responsive with gloves on, but not dramatically less than other touchscreens I’ve used. The physical buttons help, and the new layout feels more straightforward. The DURA 2 is simply easier to operate on the bike compared to the original.

The offset Garmin-style mount connection is a small but useful design feature. Larger computers can run into clearance problems with some proprietary out-front mounts. Because the DURA 2’s connection point sits farther back, I’m less concerned about that here. I tested the computer without buying COROS’s optional mount, which I appreciate having as an option because I already have a bin full of included out-front mounts that I couldn’t give away if I tried. Being able to opt out of yet another one was actually kind of refreshing.

I’ve recorded 31 hours of riding on the DURA 2, and the battery is still at 82.4%. That’s with multiple sensors paired, occasional navigation, and the screen at full brightness.

Even with the caveat that battery usage will vary from user to user based on factors like location and use case, the battery performance is extraordinary. If you regularly do rides longer than 20 hours, this is probably the computer to get. No other current head unit I’ve tested comes close to this kind of real-world endurance.

For shorter rides, the advantage is less dramatic but still useful: charging becomes one less thing to remember. And Coros deserves kudos here for maintaining battery-life performance with the DURA 2 while adding a larger screen and more processing power to the unit.

Navigation on the DURA 2 with the updated maps is a clear improvement. The faster processor makes the device feel much less sluggish when zooming or scrolling the map, and the map is easy to read while riding. Street names at tighter zoom levels are a welcome addition compared to what the original DURA offered.

My main reservation is that rerouting still depends on your phone. I get the practical argument: most of us ride with a phone anyway, and the phone can handle it. But it still feels like a shortcoming in a $500 cycling computer. Other units can reroute on their own, and I’d rather not rely on a Bluetooth phone connection when I’ve already paid for a dedicated device.

The rerouting itself is kind of hit or miss. Most of my testing has been in Southeastern Pennsylvania, and so far the DURA 2 (or, I guess I should say, the Coros app on my phone) has sent me down a trail into a stream crossing on my commuter bike only once. Following a route I designed and loaded onto the DURA 2 has gone smoothly, as expected. But I wouldn’t trust the Coros-suggested routes when navigating to a point on a map or when rerouting in an unfamiliar place.

Finally, I personally don’t mind manually loading a route onto my head unit. But in 2026, route sync should be mostly automatic. Hopefully, they can add that in a future firmware update.

Sensor pairing and ride syncing have been trouble-free for me. I’ve had no issues with the sensors I use, and activities push to the app smoothly after a ride. Which is what I expect from a core cycling computer function in 2026.

Structured training is now more than passable. I don’t use my head unit to guide workouts, but I appreciate that COROS has made the feature more useful for riders who do. You can now pause an interval without pausing the ride recording, which feels like it should have been possible from the start, but I’m always happy to see improvements.

The COROS app and Training Hub are also strengths. In some ways, the experience is simpler than Garmin Connect, and I find parts of it easier to use. You can build routes, send rides to Strava and other platforms, and see your training data alongside recovery information from a COROS watch. If you already wear a COROS watch off the bike, that integration is useful. As with Garmin Connect, though, you get the most from the system when you use the company’s hardware.

The new music controls are great, and they’re seamlessly integrated. The electronic bell sounds like an actual bike bell, which is great. But it can’t currently be paired to a bonus button on Di2 or AXS, which Coros can fix in a future firmware update.

The voice control is puzzling to me. Garmin just unveiled this feature on its latest 1060 unit, and I’m just not sure why. I’ve spent 20 years riding without talking to my cycling computer. I would much rather companies perfect their UI and button interfaces so riders can quickly and simply access the functions they need instead of implementing voice controls. I’m sure some riders will find it useful, but I can’t see myself talking to my cycling computer any time soon. Especially since every time I tried to talk to the DURA 2 while riding, it couldn’t understand me, so there's definitely room for improvement.

The DURA 2 is a much better computer than the original DURA. It has a better screen, faster maps, more responsive controls, usable training features, and a more complete app experience. Most importantly, it keeps the exceptional battery life that made the original interesting in the first place.

The price has doubled, and there's really no getting around that. I think the improvements, plus the new form factor, justify an increase. But at $499, the DURA 2 is basically the same price as the Hammerhead Karoo 3 and not much cheaper than the Garmin Edge 850. Both units have their own strengths and trade-offs, but they're polished and fully functional. By contrast, I have written the phrase “hopefully this gets fixed in a future firmware update” three times in this review.

The DURA 2’s biggest strength is that it no longer feels like a budget computer asking you to overlook its rough edges. It feels like a serious head unit with exceptional battery life, and if you regularly ride 20 hours straight, it’s the easy pick. If you don’t, the DURA 2 is still a big step forward over the original, but the rough edges still need a bit more sanding given the jump in asking price.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8918. Warrior 2 Teaches You to Balance Effort and Surrender

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Warrior 2 Pose first appeared in the May-June 2000 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Over two millennia ago, one of the most essential teachings of yoga was given on a battlefield, of all places. As recounted in the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna, the consummate warrior, becomes paralyzed with doubt and fear just as he is about to be called to action. Luckily for him, his chariot driver happens to be none other than the god Krishna, who proceeds to reveal to Arjuna the teachings of yoga to liberate him from his confusion.

In my favorite translation of the Gita, by the late scholar/teacher Eknath Easwaran (Nilgiri Press, 1985), Krishna defines yoga as “wisdom in action”—yogah karmasu kausalam (II.50). He guides Arjuna to reflect upon the source of his actions and find his internal center, where he is free from the fluctuations of the mind.

Many centuries later Mahatma Gandhi would take these teachings of the Gita as guiding principles for his life.

Gandhi saw the battlefield as a metaphor for our internal conflicts and Arjuna as the archetypal warrior within—one who sees through illusions to the truth and is able to act with courage and unwavering focus. Perhaps as a beginning yoga student, you have already encountered a glimpse of this warrior spirit in the standing pose Virabhadrasana II (or Vira II for short). In the deep lunge and open arms of this Warrior Pose variation, there is a challenging intensity—a marked contrast to the images of yoga as a passive practice intended for relaxation.

You may ask, “Why is there a Warrior Pose, when yoga is a practice of nonviolence?”

As a strong pose, Virabhadrasana II can teach modern yogis a lot about the dynamics of bringing wisdom into the actions of our everyday lives. It is a powerful pose, no doubt, but as you explore the pose’s alignment and inner attitude, the heart of the peaceful warrior begins to reveal itself.

As we go about our daily lives, we often speak of feeling “off-centered” or of needing to “get centered.” Being “centered” is a feeling of being balanced and at ease on all levels—physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually.

It is the clear space of awareness from which the wise action within any moment can be found.

To find your center in Virabhadrasana II—the place where your energy is distributed evenly, without bias—start by grounding yourself within Tadasana (Mountain Pose). The training of a spiritual warrior begins here as you let go of any external distractions and bring your awareness to your core.

When you feel your mind settle within the relaxed steadiness of Tadasana, then prepare to begin Virabhadrasana II. Consciously step your feet apart in a wide stance (4 to 5 feet), with your heels aligned parallel to one another. Pivot your left foot out to a 90-degree angle and pivot your right foot in to a 45-degree angle. Plant your feet like roots, connecting through all of the corners of your feet while lifting through the arches.

To focus on the leg work of Virabhadrasana II first, keep your arms relaxed at your sides. Slowly bend your left knee until it comes directly over your ankle. Now explore the feeling of your weight. Is all of your weight in your front leg? Lunge deeper into your left leg and then shift your weight into your back leg to feel the extremes, and then try to find the balance point.

Let your left hip sink to draw you deeper into the lunge, but keep your right leg firm, inner thigh lifting, and outer edge of your right foot reaching into the ground. As your legs develop stamina and your hips open, you can begin to explore coming into a right angle with your front leg as if you are balancing something on your thigh.

Once you find the place where your weight is evenly distributed through your legs and hips, bring your awareness to your torso. Are you collapsing into your lower back? Find your vertical center by turning your tailbone toward the earth. Without tension, lift your lower belly, the seat of your power, towards the spine. This action will awaken your center, so you can begin to extend out of your lower back and spread your chest open. Now balance your rib cage directly over your pelvis. Is your torso turning towards the left leg? Draw your right side and the top of your right thigh back to feel yourself opening out from the center.

Keep scanning your body to feel where you are losing awareness and balance. Change sides and explore Virabhadrasana II to find that even flow of energy—north, south, east, and west—throughout the pose.

As a metaphor for living, yoga can help us see how unnecessary tension within our actions shifts us off-center. To maintain Warrior Pose, we often harden our eyes, hold our breath, or shrug our shoulders. Try Virabhadrasana II again on the left side, setting up your foundation from your center. Slowly raise your arms up to shoulder height, keeping your shoulder blades pressing into and down your back. Now, turn your gaze (drishti) to the middle finger of your left hand.

Like a Zen archer spotting a bull’s-eye, who practices just holding a bow for two years before ever releasing an arrow, find balance within your focus by becoming inwardly detached.

Let the backs of your eyes look inside while you stay totally present. Feel the power of your energy radiating freely from your center. Find the balance between working to your full potential and completely relaxing, mirroring the effortless stillness of an eagle hovering over a current of wind.

As you explore this dance between being active and receptive, you can contemplate Krishna’s paradoxical teaching, “One who can see action within inaction and inaction within action is the wisest among all beings.”

As you look out from this still point and open your inner ears, you may hear your internal warrior teacher giving you insights to bring you into balance not only in this moment, but in your life as a whole. Like Arjuna as Krishna whispered over his shoulder, you may be given confidence to face your fears, courage to move forward, compassion to embrace another, and wisdom to surrender to the one who holds the reins.

Visit the Iberia Plus website and locate their published off-peak date chart for your target route. Off-peak windows typically include January through March and October through November. Confirm your travel dates fall within the off-peak range before committing points.

Log into your Iberia Plus account and search for business class award flights on your target dates. Look for flights priced at 34,000 Avios one-way. If availability is not showing, try shifting dates by 1-2 days within the off-peak window.

Once you confirm availability, transfer points from Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, Citi ThankYou, or Marriott Bonvoy. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Allow 1-2 business days for others.

Complete the booking through the Iberia website using your Avios balance. Unlike many partner awards, Iberia off-peak bookings can be made entirely online without calling. Select your seat during the booking process.

Madrid is a natural hub for onward travel. Consider booking a separate low-cost carrier flight or Avios short-haul to Barcelona, Lisbon, or Seville. Iberia's short-haul Avios pricing is also excellent for intra-Europe connections.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

You're a great fit for this redemption if:

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.

#8915. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8914. 10-Minute Morning Yoga for Strength and Surrender

Gillian E. Boult is a yoga teacher, registered social worker, psychotherapist, and author. Also an avid hiker and explorer, Gillian brings her mat into diverse landscapes, using nature as a co-regulator to soothe the nervous system, release tension, and restore cognitive focus. Here, she shares a flow in front of a waterfall.

Adding yoga to your morning routine is among the best ways to set the tone for your day. While most mornings are jammed with to-dos and getting ready rituals, taking even a few minutes to roll out your mat teaches your body, breath, and mind that presence and peace are the priority.

This 10-minute yoga practice encourages you to channel the energy of a waterfall—powerful and ever-shifting—beginning your day with strength and surrender. A series of side and forward bends, core-engaging shapes, and lower body stretches wakes up your body while reminding you of its inherent vitality.

No props are needed for this practice—just your body, your breath, and (if available) a jaw-dropping natural backdrop. If you don’t have access to nature, close your eyes when you flow allows and picture yourself in the outdoor space of your dreams, complete with sound.

Begin in a comfortable seated position, such as Easy Pose, rooting down through your sit bones. Rest your hands in your lap and either close your eyes or soften your gaze.

On your next inhalation, sweep both arms overhead and reach tall. Exhale as you take a side bend toward the left, reaching your right arm overhead as you release your left fingertips, hand, or forearm to the ground.

Inhale to come back through center. Extend your right leg out long and center your chest and hips so you’re facing your right foot. With your exhalation, hinge forward in Head-to-Knee Forward Bend, reaching any amount and resting your hands on your calf, ankle, or foot. Feel free to bend your right knee if that’s more comfortable for you.

Inhale to lift your torso, then plant your left hand behind your left hip, pressing into that hand and engaging your hips to lift in a kneeling variation of Wild Thing.

Exhale to release down to your left side body. Rest on your forearm, stack your knees, and use your right hand in front of you for support as you extend your right leg toward the sky. You might want to grab hold of your right foot or leg in this variation of Reclining Hand-to-Big-Toe.

Release your foot, slowly lowering it all the way to the ground and press through its outer edge. Inhale as you press into your left forearm and lift yourself off the mat while reaching your right arm toward the sky in a variation of Side Plank. Option to bend your bottom knee as you bring your foot behind your or to reach your top arm alongside your head.

When you’re ready, lower down to Easy Pose. Repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

With your exhalation lower down and come to a seat. Extend your legs out wide. Grow tall with your inhalation and exhale into Wide-Angled Seated Forward Bend, hinging at your hips and walking your hands forward any amount that is comfortable.

When you’re ready, walk your hands back in and carefully come onto all fours in a Tabletop position.

Once you’re settled in Tabletop, lift your right leg and guide your knee through 3 large hip circles.

Step your right foot through to land between the hands. On an inhalation, reach your arms overhead and sink deeper into your Low Lunge.

With your next exhalation, bring your hands to the mat and tuck your back toes under, straightening your right left and shifting your sit bones back in Half Splits.

When you’re ready, come back to Tabletop and repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Come back through Tabletop and widen your knees. Touch your toes together and sink your hips back in Child’s Pose. Notice how you feel in your body here, maybe setting an intention for the rest of your day. Let a word come to you.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Once you feel complete, press up to kneel in Thunderbolt Pose. Inhale your arms up overhead, and exhale to bring your hands together at heart center.

Thank yourself for taking the time to make it to your mat today.

#8913. The Biomechanics of Speed: How Your Form Can Improve Your Pace

This “speedwork” is way more fun than sprint repeats.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’re lacing up your shoes for a 5K or gearing up for a longer endurance race, if you want to get faster, you have to do both longer runs and speedwork sessions to train your aerobic and anaerobic systems. But for the biggest speed gains, you should also look beyond your cardiovascular fitness and work your… posture?

“People often think of running as a lower body sport, but running is everything going on between your ears and everywhere below,” says Anh Bui, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., a former collegiate runner, doctor of physical therapy, and biomechanics specialist in Oakland, California.

While you probably can’t (and shouldn’t) transform your running form into the stride of, say, Olympians on the podium, you can incorporate tweaks to make your mechanics more ideal for you. And that can help you improve performance, get faster, and lower your risk of getting hurt.

“There’s high variability between everyone’s biomechanics based on how you’re structurally and genetically built,” says Bui. “The key is to optimize movement, not force idealism, and to run efficiently to maximize speed and minimize injury risk.”

Read on for more about how each part of your biomechanics, from head to toe, contributes to your speed—plus a handful of moves to add to your routine that’ll help you pick up the pace.

It’s easier to maintain good posture on a short jog versus a long training run when your body starts to drag. But focusing on staying tall and keeping your shoulders from slumping is an important part of efficient running form—not to mention makes it easier to breathe.

Standing up straight as you run with a slight forward lean helps pull you forward, says Ellen Foster, D.P.T., a doctor of physical therapy, movement quality expert, and running coach in Cincinnati. “I like to encourage runners to sort of ‘fall’ forward from the ankles so that their hips are slightly in front of their feet,” she says. “Just make sure you don’t lean forward by bending at the hips or waist, as that would lead to pushing your hips back and losing valuable hip extension.”

Your arms play a surprisingly big role in picking up your pace. Just try pumping your arms harder next time you’re huffing up a hill and see how much it helps. Here’s why: The motion of your arms and legs are linked. “And our arms act as pendulums to help balance our trunk, as forces travel up our body from our legs,” says Foster. “So, when we swing our arms in a more efficient way, our legs often follow their lead.”

While research on just how crucial the arm swing is to running mechanics is limited (most studies focus more on the lower half of the body), and results offer mixed information, most researchers agree that swinging the arms helps with vertical oscillation (or how much we move upward as we stride), side-to-side balance, and minimizing rotation.

“Anecdotally, I find that arm swing drills can be a good starting place when working on increasing cadence, especially if someone is struggling to increase cadence due to poor coordination,” Foster says. Cadence, or the number of steps you take per minute, often changes depending on the speed you’re running, but experts suggest a quicker cadence can limit overstriding and help with forward momentum.

Sprinters tend to drive their knees up aggressively, about 90 degrees from the ground. That’s not sustainable over longer distances, says Bui, who says distance runners should ideally maintain more like 45 degrees of knee drive.

Why does the position of your knees matter? “Picking up your speed without appropriate knee drive will increase likelihood of overstriding, or landing with the foot far in front of your body,” Bui explains. That can slow you down and increases ground reaction forces—or forces exerted by the ground onto the body, Bui says—and ups your chances of injury.

When considering how your feet play into your form and your pace, a lot of it is about those ground reaction forces. If you reduce the time your feet come in contact with the ground, you can potentially lower the force on your body—and lessen your risk of injuries like shin splints, says Foster.

“When we look at vertical ground reaction forces (vGRF) across time, midfoot striking has a lower rate of vGRF with one smooth peak,” Bui explains. By contrast, heel striking has a longer ground contact time, leading to a higher peak force and greater load on the body. This is because your ankle dorsiflexors (when you pull toes toward shins) can’t efficiently absorb the impact of your foot strike, and therefore, your knee joint takes on extra force, she adds.

Try to pick up your cadence and adjust so you’re striking the ground with your foot underneath your body (rather than out too far in front) to help reduce those forces up the leg. Typically, heel striking accompanies overstriding—which can increase risk of injury from the added load—and upping your cadence can help you avoid it.

Keep in mind that your body needs time to adjust to any changes you make in your form. Also, while your body may take on more force with a heel strike, it doesn’t always lead to more injuries or slower speeds. It’s one piece of the biomechanical puzzle. “Heel striking isn’t inherently dangerous by itself,” Foster says.

To improve your biomechanics, working with a run-form coach or physical therapist with advanced training in motor learning or neuromuscular re-education is hugely beneficial, says Foster. “It’s easy to understand the correct biomechanics, but it’s much more challenging to implement them,” she says.

Although working with one of these pros is ideal, a few exercises you can practice on your own can help you get a jumpstart on improving biomechanics.

Here are five biomechanical drills that focus on different aspects of your form. Do them often (for a few minutes as part of your warmup before every run, for example) to make the movements feel like second nature. Then, when you’re working to incorporate tweaks to your form into your run, don’t try to make several changes all at once; try sprinkling them into your runs slowly, thinking about a single form tweak for 30 seconds once per mile.

Just make sure not to jump in too quickly. All tweaks to your body’s biomechanics should be gradual or you risk the chance of injury, says Foster.

Why it works: This super-quick drill emphasizes balance and stability while firing up your posterior chain, which helps develop a more powerful push-off.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Raise right knee to hip height. In a quick, explosive movement, lower right foot to floor and raise left knee high, then lower left knee and raise right knee to hip height again. Do 5 reps. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: Practicing this movement at a quick, consistent pace helps make your arm swing more efficient.

How to do it: Set a metronome app (like Metronome Beats) to a beats per minute that feels in sync with your running cadence; 180 bpm is ideal but dial it back if that feels too quick. Sitting on the edge of a chair or standing with feet hip-width apart, pump arms forward and back to the beat, starting with 10-15 seconds. Do 3-5 sets, resting for about 10-20 second between sets.

Why it works: The plyometric motion of this jump helps prep your tendons to store and release energy quickly. Start by doing the move with both legs, then progress to one leg at a time, recommends Bui.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Keeping legs straight, push off the floor from the ball of feet and swing arms up to jump as high as you can. As soon as you land, jump again. Do 5 reps, jumping as quickly as you can (and minimizing your feet’s contact with the floor). Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: This quick movement increases tendon capacity, trains your body to absorb load as you make contact with the ground, and decreases the time your feet stay in contact with the ground.

How to do it: Stand on the edge of a step or box about a foot tall. With right foot leading, step both feet down to floor. As soon as left foot hits floor, jump up explosively, pushing off floor with both feet. Repeat for 5 steps. Then repeat with left foot leading the step down. Do 2 sets.

Why it works: This move is really just running, with exaggerated motions that mimic ideal sprinting form—and helps develop speed, power, and explosiveness.

How to do it: On a track or long patch of ground, jog forward with as long a stride as possible. As you move, raise the front knee as high as possible while lifting the back foot (keeping leg straight) behind you. Continue for 10 reps total. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Recommended Experience: No experience necessary! Anyone can accomplish this training plan.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: This plan is for a new runner who is just getting back into exercise.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a new runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This plan peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For runners comfortable exercising for at least an hour at a moderate effort. This plan peaks at 32 miles in a week with a 14-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a consistent runner used to regularly working out four to five times a week. The plan starts with a 10-mile long run and peaks at 44 to 47 miles a week with a 22-mile long run, helping you average under a 9:10 per mile come race day.
