#8893. Don’t Let a Flat Tire End Your Ride. Here’s What I Carry in My Ride-Rescue Kit

A practical guide to building a flat kit that gets you home without overloading your bike.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are so many options out there when setting up a flat tire kit. During my time in bike shops I sold every flat kit you could imagine—from the basic prepackaged flat repair kits to repair kits that could fix almost anything on the bike. When you have the right pieces of gear, it can make the difference between an easy roadside fix and finding a plan B to get home.

Building the right kit can make the difference between fixing the bike mid-ride and needing an unexpected pickup. One key is bringing the things you need and not what you don’t—then knowing how to use the tools in your kit.

Even on bikes you’ve had for a while it can be worth revisiting what’s sitting in your flat pack. Below I’ll walk you through what’s in my basic flat kit, why I pick those pieces, and why you should intermittently check out your flat pack to prevent any roadside surprises.

The tire levers are the foundation of any good flat repair kit—after all, you won’t be able to fix a flat very well if you can’t get the tire off and back on. I’ve gone through many different lever options over the years in my own flat kits, as well as from my time running a bike shop. The tire levers I swear by are the Pedro’s yellow tire levers. They are burly enough to be reliable and durable—I’m rarely worried about snapping a Pedro’s lever even on a tight tire.

The one thing many people don’t think about with levers is that sometimes you drop them or put them down when you’re trying to manage the roadside repair. The Pedro’s levers are easy to find thanks to their bright yellow color.

One runner-up is the tire lever from Muc-Off. They are similar in size, durability, and come in bright and easy to find colors. Personally I have not had the same amount of time using Muc-Off levers compared to the Pedro’s levers. One final tip: don’t use metal levers. Yes, they are burly, but they can easily damage rims when trying to get a tire off—especially carbon.

The traditional tube you may have gotten the last time you stopped in your local shop while picking up a tube to fix a flat at home is a great option to put in your flat pack, but there are other options. TPU and latex tubes are popular because of their light weight and small packed size.

I typically go with a standard tube on most of my flat kits. This is because I typically ride all year round and some of those lighter and more packable materials for tubes are more sensitive to temperature. If you’re a fair-weather rider, however, it can be worth considering a TPU or latex tube. Just remember to double-check that both the tube and valve size are correct for the wheels you are using.

One note on checking out your tubes: check to make sure the tube is in good condition every few months. I was on a ride recently where someone got a flat and his multitool was against the tube in his saddle bag. The multitool rubbed a hole into the side of the tube making it useless. He said he had not inspected that tube in at least a year. Luckily we had an extra tube for him and could keep rolling, but a quick check could have prevented him pulling a tube from someone else’s flat kit.

Similar to tire levers, I’ve used many different inflators over the years. My favorites to use are either the PDW CO2 inflator or the Muc-Off Inflator. These two options are durable and are easy to use with gloves on—which is especially helpful as we get into some cooler temperatures.

I carry two cans of CO2 because I’ve run into several experiences before where one ends up not being enough. It could be because I used one to try to add a burst of air in the hopes my tubeless system would fill the hole with sealant and I could go on my way. I’ve also had user error experiences where I simply didn’t get the canister on correctly and most or all of the air rushed out of the canister. In any case, they don’t take up much space, but having a backup is a key piece of the flat kit.

There are other inflation options you can go with too. Electronic pumps have been growing in popularity over the last few years, with test editor Dan Chabanov recently calling out the Cycplus AS2 Ultra Electric Inflator as his inflator of choice. I typically add a frame-mounted pump on longer rides, because these can’t run out of battery and as long as you can still pump you won’t run out of available air.

You’d be surprised what you can fix with a few zip ties. I’ve used these packable and inexpensive additions to fix issues like broken bottle cage bolts and broken cable and housing guides. I’ve had friends who have reattached things like derailleurs and saddle bags with a few strategically placed zip ties.

When I ride I typically carry a $10 bill and a single dollar bill. I know $11 seems like a random amount of money to carry on the bike. But the single and the ten serve two different purposes. A single dollar bill works as a great tire boot if you have a large gash in your tire. Simply put the dollar bill inside the tire against the gash before putting the tube in. If you run tubeless you can apply a little sealant from inside the tire to the dollar bill to help it stick better against the tire. Then when you inflate your tube, the pressure of the tube inside the tire will keep the dollar bill in place. The dollar bill will protect the tube from the elements and the road surface outside the tire.

The ten-dollar bill is your backup plan. I’ve been on rides before where I underestimated the amount of hydration and nutrition I needed to get through an effort. Having a few dollars for a gas station or convenience store refuel stop has dragged me out of the hole more than once. Most places these days take digital forms of payment like Apple Pay, but if you’re riding in more remote areas cash can be king.

A multitool that has the basic Allen keys and screwdriver that you’ll need is essential. If it has sizes 4, 5, and 6 you’ll be able to take care of most roadside fixes or adjustments you might ride into.

I personally like to bring a multitool with a chain breaker because I’ve had to fix a chain more than once on a ride. If fixing a chain is something you want to be prepared for on your ride, consider bringing a quick link that is compatible with your chain. They are another small and relatively inexpensive addition to your flat kit that can save plenty of headaches. A broken chain doesn’t have to be the end of your ride if you have the tools and the knowledge to piece it back together.

Different bikes have different ways to carry all this stuff. Some bikes have internal frame storage, some saddles have integrated mounts for certain bags, and some bikes have dropper posts that are only compatible with select saddle bags. On really short road rides I’ve even just thrown the basics of my flat kit in a jersey pocket. Personally, I typically put my flat repair kit into a frame bag, saddle bag, or utilize the internal frame storage so I can keep the extra weight and bulk off my body. If you have any essentials in your flat kit that I don’t include in mine let me know in the comments below.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

But switching to an electric cargo bike has made the biggest positive impact on my overall quality of life. Thanks to a cargo bike, I’ve been mostly car-free for the last several months.

Traditional bicycles are great for your daily commute, running errands, and cruising around. However, if you need to carry more than you can squeeze into a backpack or maybe some panniers, most commuter bikes or e-bikes aren’t up for the job. Common tasks like grocery shopping, carrying large items, or transporting children can be tough on even the best of them. That’s what makes cargo bikes great—they can carry everything (and more!) that you can imagine.

As their name suggests, cargo bikes are designed to carry heavy, large, or awkward loads. Their extra hauling capacity makes cargo bikes incredibly useful for families, commuters, and riders in cities, suburbs, and small towns across the country. Bicycle brands produce cargo bikes in several distinct layouts to meet the needs of riders seeking to carry or move more stuff by pedal power.

Almost any bicycle purpose-built to carry passengers or extra gear—such as packages, bags, or boxes—can be called a “cargo bike.” Cargo bikes typically feature reinforced frames, racks or mounting points, and come with higher payload capacities than traditional commuter, city, or townie bikes. Bike brands and third-party manufacturers also offer a wide array of accessories to outfit a cargo bike for your specific needs and use cases.

Bicycling’s editors are huge fans of cargo bikes, and we use them regularly for our daily commutes, running errands, dropping kids at school, and family rides. Like other bicycle types, cargo bikes come in all shapes and sizes—and there’s almost certainly one that’s perfect for you. Finally, while non-assisted cargo bikes are available, electric-assist cargo bikes are now far more common. So all of the models we test use electric motors.

Buying Tip: Consider where you will store your cargo bike. Their large size and extra weight can make cargo bikes difficult to store if you don’t have a garage or dedicated bike storage. If you need to park your cargo bike outside, get a heavy-duty bike lock and a bicycle cover to keep it safe.

Some cargo bikes are loaded with features but cost too much, while others are low-priced but don’t ride well. However, the Aventon Abound LR is the rare $2,000 electric cargo bike that doesn’t feel like a compromise—And that’s why it’s our Best Overall pick.

The Abound LR is built to handle daily life—daycare drop-offs and pickups, grocery runs, and commuting—without the premium price tag of its competitors. Plus, it rides with more polish than some bikes costing twice as much. This makes it a great option for families and utility‑minded riders. The LR can handle kids, panniers, and weekly shopping trips without stretching the budget. It’s ideal for those who value comfort and stability over top‑end speed.

If you’re comparing this Aventon to other electric cargo bikes, it feels more polished than budget longtails like the Lectric Xpedition 2.0 and Rad Power’s Rad Wagon 5. Yet, the Abound LR costs far less than premium mid‑drive cargo rigs from Tern, Cannondale, and Trek.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it’s one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around. The dual-battery model ($1,799) boasts an incredible 120-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. This makes the XPedition an option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

However, concessions had to be made somewhere to reach this low price, and the result is a somewhat cheap feel. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but it is erratic at times. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend.

Tern’s Quick Haul Long is enticing because it delivers the core functionality of the pricier GSD series at a lower price. While the Quick Haul Long’s frame isn’t as sleek as the GSD and lacks a suspension fork, the bike still has everything needed to be a true car replacement.

The Quick Haul features include hydraulic disc brakes, a robust double kickstand, a built-in frame lock, trailer attachment points, and an impressive maximum weight limit of 419 pounds. Tern also offers a wide range of accessories to customize the bike to your individual needs. Even when loaded with two kids and a trailer full of groceries, the Bosch Cargo Line motor handles the load with ease. However, don’t expect a speedy ride when fully laden. The bike can handle the load (and you’ll get where you want to go), but it won’t zip to its maximum pedal-assist speed of 20 mph when weighed down.

If you like the look, features, and price of Aventon’s Abound LR but want a smaller package, the SR is the bike for you. The SR has the same 440-pound carrying capacity and 60-mile range as its longtail sibling, but on a shorter wheelbase chassis. This makes it ideal for riders with space constraints (such as apartments and RVs) or anyone seeking a quick ride around town.

The Specialized Globe Haul ST packs 419 pounds of cargo capacity into a surprisingly compact frame. With powerful brakes, dialed geometry, and well-thought-out features, it’s ready for commuting, grocery getting, neighborhood errands, or getting a child to daycare. Without active suspension, the Haul relies on massive 3.5-inch tires for its ride comfort, which work well on all but the roughest roads.

My partner, Julia, purchased a Haul ST after reading the Bike of the Year review. She uses it for commuting in Boston and describes the Haul as zippy. She said, “The power levels are flexible, and I can easily adjust them to how I want to ride or tackle hills.” She also likes the cargo configurations for carrying groceries and running errands. Julia also likes the Haul’s geometry; “It’s nice to ride upright, and it gives me more visibility.”

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

The Fetch+ 4 is Trek’s take on the classic Dutch bakfiets. This bike is essentially the minivan of bikes—it carries up to four kids. It includes two child seats, but you can add accessories to improve your passengers’ comfort. These include a full cover for the basket to keep everyone out of the wind and rain. To power the Fetch, Trek uses Bosch’s BES3 system with a Bosch Cargo Drive motor. It delivers power via a Gates Carbon belt drive for virtually maintenance-free operation.

Most families know Radio Flyer for its iconic red wagons, tricycles, and ride-on toys, but did you know the company also made a range of electric bikes? I use “made” here because, unfortunately, Flyer is backing away from e-bikes to concentrate on its core business. However, if you buy this bike, you’ll still have after-purchase support and the brand will have spare parts available.

The Loop is a 20-inch-wheel mid-tail model equipped with a 750W hub motor (87Nm torque) and can carry up to two children as passengers. Like a good family bike, Flyer loads the Loop with safety features, including a fully enclosed rear wheel, long front fender, turn signals, and four-piston Magura hydraulic disc brakes. Flyer offers the Loop in one universal frame size (fitting riders 4’11” to 6’3”) and four color choices.

Health & Fitness Editor Monique LeBrun tested the Loop with her six-year-old daughter for several months. “I’ve never ridden an e-bike before, so I was a little skeptical about it, but I really enjoy riding the Radio Flyer,” she said. Lebrun notes that “the seat is very comfortable, and I love that it has a low frame so I can easily step on and off the bike.”

The Tern GSD redefines what a car-replacement bike can be. It’s easy to picture running errands on a cargo bike if you live in a city or a town with great cycling infrastructure. However, many people live in suburbs or other areas not exactly designed for bike commuting. The GSD’s Class 3 Bosch pedal-assist motor, massive cargo capacity, and solid battery range make long hauls realistic, even for riders who live miles from town.

Riders from 5 feet to 6’6” can share the same bike, thanks to quick-release adjustments on the seatpost and handlebar. The bar can even rotate forward for tall riders who want extra reach. The bike also features premium touches you won’t find on low-cost cargo bikes—like a suspension fork, Magura 4-piston hydraulic brakes, an integrated lock, and a suspension seatpost. Practical design details make storage and transport surprisingly manageable: the handlebar folds at the headset, the seat drops quickly, and the whole bike can be tipped upright to rest on its rear rack—perfect for tight garage corners. However, be aware that the GSD’s extra weight can make loading it into a vehicle a two-person task.

Do you need to carry absolutely everything and want to do it in style? If so, an Urban Arrow might be right for you.

This front-loader, basket-style cargo bike is designed for families and people carrying large items like multiple kids, large dogs (plural), a Costco run, or a couch—All things people can carry with an Urban Arrow. Thanks to its 75 Nm Bosch Cargo Line motor and 545Wh battery, it has the torque and range to carry you and your stuff up hills and to your destination without breaking a sweat.

Domestic and international cargo bike popularity has exploded in the past decade, says Xtracycles founder and longtail cargo bike pioneer Ross Evans. There are generally four main styles of cargo bikes: longtail, short-tail, front loader, and the bakfiet (a Dutch term that translates to ‘box bike’). You can also find trike varieties for riders needing to transport heavy loads or more than two children.

➡️ Longtail cargo bikes are the most agile and lightweight design. They transport cargo or passengers on an extended tail section behind the rider.

➡️ Short-tail cargo bikes are a variant of longtail bikes, but with a shorter rear extension that makes them more compact and better suited for those tight on space.

➡️ Front loader bikes place the payload in front of the rider, generally on a low-slung platform adaptable to suit many needs.

➡️ Bakfiet-style bikes feature a large basket (typically in front of the rider) for carrying cargo or transporting multiple passengers.

Moving hundreds of pounds on a bike without a motor is great...if you want to get a workout. But most riders and families don’t want that stress or extra work. That’s why we recommend electric motor-equipped cargo bikes. “Electricity and cargo bikes go together like PB&J,” Evans says. E-cargo bikes feature pedal-assist electric motors that can deliver more than 50 miles of range. This makes cargo bikes more accessible to riders who want car-like convenience in a bike-sized package.

However, the tech comes at a price: Electric cargo bikes are pricier than their non-electric counterparts. Unless you live somewhere completely flat, we think an e-cargo bike is the best choice. Electric motors vastly improve a cargo bike’s usability and can save you money in the long run by making it a more effective car substitute.

Once you’ve purchased a cargo bike, you’ll want the right accessories to maximize its utility. Start on the manufacturer’s website: Many brands sell panniers, racks, and child seats to match their cargo bikes. Alternatively, if your style is more “dump it and go,” bakfiets use a single spacious box—typically upfront—that’ll fit all your stuff (there are still seat belts for your kids). The best way to determine which style or bike you prefer is to take bikes for test rides.

Approach an e-cargo bike and accessory purchase the same way you would if buying a car. Try and test as many options as possible. Prioritize your most common cargo needs. While it can be fun to think in aspirational terms, a bike suited to your daily needs means you use it more often.

These bikes are thoroughly put through their paces by the Bicycling test team. We don’t only test them—we live with them. We haul groceries, drop kids off at school, and squeeze in as many rides as possible to see if these e-cargo bikes can truly replace our cars for daily life. Test Editor Dan Chabanov puts them through the ultimate car-replacement experiment on the streets of his hometown of Philadelphia, and Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy tests them on her daily commute to the office. A

t our Easton, Pennsylvania headquarters, the rest of the team gives these bikes a daily beating, using them to run errands around town (because let’s be honest—e-cargo bikes are just plain fun to ride). We also speak with the product managers behind the designs to understand their choices, and compare each model to its closest competitors to see how they stack up. Bottom line: we test these bikes like we’d use them in real life—because we actually did.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8890. The 6 Best Walking Pads for Staying Active During the Workday

Improve your focus and get your steps in seamlessly with one of these walking pads.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Stuck at your desk all day? Us, too—and we work for a running publication. (Oh, the irony!) Well, fret not, fellow office warriors: Walking pads and under-desk treadmills are here to save the day—and boost your step count. These low-profile treadmills slide right under your standing desk, making it easy to walk and work at the same time. Thanks to a renewed focus on health, whether you’re working from home or heading into the office, walking pads have quickly become a staple in home offices and shared workspaces alike. So, whether you’re aiming to close those rings or boost your daily steps, a walking pad can help you stay active throughout the workday without missing that 3 p.m. meeting.

🏃🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Walking for Weight Loss Guide can make it happen!

Recent studies support the benefits of movement while working: office employees using treadmill desks have reported improved energy, greater focus, and a boosted mood over just a few months of consistent use. Plus, the convenience of walking pads means you can exercise regardless of the weather or your schedule—no gym membership required. With so many walking pads on the market, each offering a unique blend of features and portability, at a range of prices, finding the right model can be overwhelming. Not to worry, though. We put tens of thousands of steps on these machines to find the best ones for you.

If you’re looking for portability, a cushioned deck, affordability, and a walking pad you can use while you’re in the office without people on your meeting hearing your treadmill? This is the one for you. We’ve had it at HQ for years, and it’s consistently in use by our team. It has seen thousands of miles, and it’s still going.

It’s got a well-cushioned deck that absorbs impact, a motor built for heavier walkers, and it’s relatively wide for a walking pad. It is, however, a bit short front-to-back, but it’s fine for most people. If you’re a giant like my brother? You might want a different model, otherwise, this is just about perfect.

If your social feeds are overflowing with DeerRun under-desk walking pads, you’re not alone. This TikTok-famous gadget is everywhere, and for good reason: It’s a simple, space-saving treadmill that you can control with a remote or an app.

The app’s got your back, letting you dial up the speed without breaking a sweat (or your focus). And topping out at just over 3 mph, it’s more of a gentle stroll than a full-on sprint.

The deck’s a cozy—if kinda tight—35 by 16 inches, which means it’ll tuck neatly under your desk. It’s easy to use and that glorious cushioned feel is pure bliss for your feet while you’re getting those steps in.

This is our office’s new BFF. The most frequent user, Hype Director Aly Ellis, said that her favorite feature is the convenience, noting “I prefer this one to one with arms because it allows me to adjust the desk height when I need to for comfort purposes.” She’s also a big fan of the fact that it lights up, but mostly because it’s cool. I agree. She does worry about losing the remote, as we all do, but fun fact! You can operate it via the app, so there’s no real worry there.

It’s quiet and sturdy, has a 12 percent incline, and has a high weight limit, so larger-bodied walkers should feel comfortable on this walking pad.

This is easily the most compact on this list. It folds up to about the size of a queen blanket, but it doesn’t feel flimsy or cheap. WalkingPad has made it its business to build high-quality walking pads that are made for your home or office.

I like this one because it’s no fuss, no muss, has a large 48-inch by 16-inch walking surface, weighs only 50 pounds, and it’s whisper quiet.

The Urevo Strol 2.0 walking pad is the under-desk treadmill you want if you tend toward boredom. It has a ton of built-in programming, and the ability to connect to a ton more like Zwift.

Once you link the app to your phone, you can control everything right there. But, if that’s not your style, traditional controls are easy to access and use. It’s a smooth walk, quieter than previous models, and you can move it around easily.

The combination of the sturdy tablet holder and smart app integration creates a user-friendly experience that blends exercise with productivity or entertainment effortlessly in any space.

If you’ve ever wondered how hard you can push yourself while you work, do I have the walking pad for you. This puppy inclines all the way to 14 percent, which—whoa—and it does it with the power of a brushless motor, which makes it quieter (though it can’t quiet your huffing and puffing), and that same motor will last a lot longer than others thanks to its construction.

The whole thing is remote controlled, so when you’re fighting for your life and you don’t want your Teams meeting to see it, you can quickly adjust on the fly.

When shopping for the best under-desk walking pad, keep these factors in mind:

Size and Portability: Ensure the walking pad’s dimensions fit under your desk and in your workspace. Consider weight and whether the machine has wheels for easy storage or movement.

Belt Size: Wider belts provide more stability and comfort, while narrower pads are better for tight spaces. Longer deck lengths work best for those with a longer stride.

Speed Range: Most walking pads offer speeds from 0.5 to 4 mph—enough for gentle walking to brisk paces. Some 2-in-1 pads allow faster speeds when used away from a desk.

Incline Options: A few models feature adjustable inclines for varied intensity, though many are flat for multitasking. If you want more of a workout, look for pads with at least a minor incline capability.

Weight Capacity: Check each machine’s weight limit, especially if you need extra support or want a more robust frame.

Noise Level: Choose a quiet pad for minimal distraction, particularly if you share your space with others or take calls frequently.

Ease of Use: Look for simple controls (often via remote) and clear displays. Consider features like app compatibility, folding capabilities, and maintenance requirements.

Price: Budget models are available for under $200, while high-end or commercial-grade options cost significantly more. Decide which features are worth extra investment for your specific needs.

So, what’s the difference between a treadmill and a walking pad? There are a lot of parallels for sure, and functionally they’re very similar. However, the real difference between a treadmill and a walking pad happens under the hood. Walking pads have smaller, quieter motors that don’t allow you to pick up the pace dramatically, but they keep them quiet enough to use while you work or read. They’re also a lot lower to the ground, and that low step height makes them a great choice for folks who have joint and mobility issues. They’re shorter and narrower than traditional treadmills so that they fit easily under desks. Luckily, they’re also easier to store, and many of them fold into little packages or can be stored on their side. And the point many people love the most? They’re usually a lot cheaper.

Our team performed all walking pad testing either in our offices for hundreds of hours or in our own homes, reflecting the real-world environments where these products are most used. Each unit was assessed with a focus on:

Speed and Incline: We measured each pad’s speed range and, where available, incline adjustments, making sure transitions were smooth and controls responsive.

Noise: We operated pads during conference calls and regular work to evaluate how quietly each model ran.

Design and Portability: We checked for ease of setup, the ability to move and store the pad, and whether the design fit under multiple desk types.

User Experience: Testers of varying heights and stride lengths used each pad for sessions extending beyond an hour, noting comfort, usability, and any unique features or challenges.

Every product featured here was rigorously tested for durability, performance, and portability in the Runner’s World offices and in the homes of our editors, ensuring our recommendations are both practical and trustworthy. Whether you’re a remote worker, student, or just trying to reduce your sedentary hours, our comprehensive guide will help you find the best under-desk walking pad to fit your space and support your movement goals.

Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#8889. How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

This story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

My mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

This was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the plans I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

On June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

#8888. Zwift+ Adds a Virtual Coach and Real Roads to Your Indoor Rides

Zwift+ introduces a new subscription tier with an adaptive plan and real-road video. I tried both.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Since its 2015 debut, Zwift has focused on indoor riding in a gamified virtual world. Now the company is nudging riders toward the real world, too. Zwift+ introduces a new subscription tier with two big features: a virtual coach that sometimes tells you to ride outdoors, and video routes that let your avatar ride real roads while you stay indoors.

I’ve got all the details, along with my first impressions of riding the new routes and working with Coach.

Let me guess: You heard “new subscription tier,” sucked your teeth, and thought, “Oh, great. Another subscription. *Sigh* How much?” Friend, I feel you.

In the U.S., Zwift+ costs $29.99 a month, $10 more than the standard Zwift membership. It includes all the standard Zwift membership features, plus Coach and Video.

You can’t add just Coach or Video separately: they are a package deal. But the company says you can move between the standard membership and Zwift+ easily and as often as you like.

The standard Zwift membership remains $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year.

First of the two new big features in Zwift+ is Coach. It’s an adaptable virtual coaching service that builds easy-to-understand training plans.

Zwift isn’t going after the TrainingPeaks power user or even the AI-powered CoachCat audience. It is aimed at Zwifters who ride about three to eight hours a week and want more structure and a personalized plan without hiring a personal coach.

Coach lives in the Companion app. To build a plan, you answer a few straightforward questions: your experience level (recreational, amateur, competitive, or elite); your goal (train for an event, build endurance or speed, burn calories, or improve climbing); plan length (four, eight, or 12 weeks); how many hours you can ride each week; which days you’re available; and which day you can set aside for a longer ride.

Then it crunches a few 1s and 0s and spits out a plan.

While the shorthand version is that AI generates the plans, Zwift describes the planning engine as machine learning, a subset of artificial intelligence. Zwift says the plan comes from a training model grounded in peer-reviewed sports science and uses anonymized power and heart-rate data from millions of Zwift riders. It then adjusts the result to your goal, recent fitness, schedule, and riding preferences. The company says the model was tested against more than 65 million Zwift rides from 2025 and considers dozens of possible sessions when building a plan.

“The plan itself follows clear rules, so we can trace recommendations back to the reasons behind them. That was deliberate so that you can know why Coach tells you to ride something,” Mark Cote, Zwift’s head of product, told me.

The plans are Zwift-forward, naturally. They prescribe Zwift’s workouts, routes, RoboPacers, and events, with the occasional outdoor ride mixed in. Zwift says 63 percent of its riders do a variety of activities, while only 13 percent stick exclusively to structured workouts. Coach embraces variety and isn’t just weeks of ERG grind sessions.

Once your plan is set, you can see the schedule in the Companion app and the main app’s home screen. After the ride, you get feedback in a new Coach Analysis tab on the activity report. You can also check it later in Companion.

You can make changes in Companion, too: schedule a different Zwift ride or event, add an outdoor ride, or log a rest day or time away. Based on your changes, Coach can then adapt the plan at your request.

It can also notice when your week goes differently than planned. For example, if you take a rest day instead of doing a workout, record an outdoor ride through a linked service such as Garmin, or go too hard during an event, Coach may prompt you to adapt the plan. If you accept, it adjusts the plan.

Zwift says recovery data from services such as WHOOP and Oura can shape the wording of Coach’s messages, but a low recovery score won’t automatically change your prescribed workout. Coach Chat, an AI chatbot that would let you ask questions about the plan conversationally, is a future feature. It won’t be available at launch.

One noteworthy shortcoming of Zwift Coach: You can’t push Zwift workouts to a GPS head unit to perform them outdoors. That said, there are fairly easy ways to take the bones of a specific Zwift workout and make something that can live on your Hammerhead or Garmin head unit.

I’ve been using a beta version of Coach for a few weeks now. I’ve found it admirably easy to set up, use, and adapt. It’s all very Zwifty, with lots of colors, iconography, and cheery, easy-to-digest language.

The plans and workouts (Zwift has recently updated its library with dozens of new workouts) seem well considered, but I don’t have enough time with Coach to know how effective it is at lifting my performance.

For someone taking their first steps toward structured training and feedback, I think Zwift Coach is a brilliant entry point, and I feel even more experienced cyclists looking to improve their performance will appreciate how easy and user-friendly Coach is.

The second highlight new feature is Zwift Video. It adds real roads to the game: Your avatar rides over footage recorded on actual routes, with familiar Zwift physics and game features layered on top.

At launch, 21 routes across six countries total 385 kilometers (239 miles) of roads. The routes range from 6.2 to 29 kilometers (about 3.9 to 18 miles) and include the French Alps, Mallorca, Tenerife, the Western Cape, Lofoten, southern Utah, Colorado, and the Scottish Highlands. Zwift says it will begin adding more routes regularly in the new year.

Zwift employees have recorded the footage specifically for Zwift’s video routes. Playback speeds up or slows down with your avatar, and like classic Zwift, you’ll still see other Zwifter avatars and find all the familiar Zwift features, including drafting, segment leaderboards, HoloReplay, PowerUps, Ride Ons, Drops, XP, and badges. Pack dynamics and road surfaces retain the same ride characteristics as in Zwift’s classic graphics-based worlds. Surfaces range from smooth pavement to broken pavement and gravel, with different rolling resistance.

The main restriction is that video routes are one-way. You can’t make a U-turn, and the roads don’t loop. Reach the end, and you are teleported back to the start where your ride continues uninterrupted.

I’ve ridden a few of the video routes so far. The rideplay is familiar Zwift, so it’s really just a change of scenery. And beautiful scenery it is. I’ve ridden a few of these routes in the real world, and while they can’t compare with the real thing, they are still often breathtaking in Zwift. There’s plenty to see, including quirky little details that I’m certain will become part of Zwift lore.

One welcome change is how Zwift marks the start of segments. Large chevrons “painted” on the road alert you to an approaching segment, and barriers and more chevrons clearly mark the start line. It’s a huge improvement over the sometimes easy-to-miss segment starts in Zwift’s classic worlds. I asked a Zwift representative whether classic-world segments might get similar treatment, and they said it was under consideration.

A couple of details take some getting used to. Cars and trucks appear in the footage. Zwift says it curates the footage to reduce traffic, but the roads aren’t traffic-free; however, the traffic doesn’t influence the game’s physics.

Climbing also looks different. I found that a 10 percent grade on a video route looked much less steep than the same grade in a classic Zwift world. A Zwift representative told me classic routes visually exaggerate grades, roughly doubling them, so the climbs read clearly on screen. Video footage doesn’t get that treatment, and the camera can flatten the terrain.

At launch, Video won’t have meetups or scheduled events, but Zwift says those will arrive in the coming months.

Now you might be thinking, wait, didn’t Zwift buy Rouvy, an indoor riding and training service built around real-world video routes? It did. But even though Zwift owns Rouvy, these aren’t Rouvy routes. Zwift representatives told me the video routes were filmed exclusively for Zwift and that the two services will continue independently, with their own content and features. They said there are no plans to bring Rouvy content to Zwift or fold Rouvy into the platform.

Zwift+ isn’t the only change coming. Zwift is also refreshing the Companion home screen, adding WHOOP and Oura connections, and introducing Watt Lock, an ERG-style control that lets you lock onto a target power during free rides.

Zwift also opened The Wild Isles, a new Watopia expansion, on October 26. Inspired by California’s coast and Catalina Island, it adds three islands and about 17 kilometers of flat roads between the Mayan Jungle and Jarvis Island. The new roads create a bypass around the Jungle and include nine cycling routes and three running routes, with ocean views and wildlife such as bison, whales, and egrets.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#8885. How Runner’s World Training Plans Helped Four Runners Crush the New York City Marathon

Their stories will inspire you to train for your best marathon.

Among the more than 61,000 runners who crossed the finish line of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon were 18 Runner’s World+ members who were part of the Race With Runner’s World+ team. Two were first-time marathoners while 16 others set big goals, such as adding to their World Marathon Major collection and hitting new PRs. No matter their specific ambition, some team members used these Runner’s World+ training plans to power themselves to the Central Park finish line.

Whatever your goal distance and time, you can find a plan by exploring our full training plan collection, including the ones our members used to return to the marathon, earn a sixth star, and run a PR.

🏃‍♀️ Want to run some of the best races in the country with us? Bookmark our Race With Runner’s World+ program page, which gives Runner’s World+ members of all backgrounds and levels a chance at free entry into select races.

Prior to New York, 46-year-old Erin Dewalt ran her last marathon in 2022, a race that she described as a “disaster.” Then, she finished in more than four hours and had an overall rough race day experience.

After a four-year marathon hiatus, Dewalt knew she needed a smart training plan to ensure she would arrive prepared for the NYC Marathon start line. The RW Break 3:45 plan aligned well with her weekly training volume of around four runs per week. For inspiration, she printed the calendar and stuck it to her fridge, checking off completed runs and moving workouts as needed.

The result for Dewalt in the Big Apple? A 3:26:18 marathon performance—breaking the 3:45 barrier by nearly 20 minutes. “I was spot on [with hitting my goal],” Dewalt said after crossing the finish line. “I wanted to enjoy it and have fun but also run around three and a half hours.”

Like Dewalt, Scott Shellabarger printed a Runner’s World training plan, but he used the Break 3:15 plan. In fact, he used it for two races: the NYC Marathon in November and the Flying Pig Marathon in his hometown of Cincinnati, Ohio, in May. “I actually used it for the last marathon I ran, for the Flying Pig, and that’s where I got my PR at,” Shellabarger said. “The training plans are fantastic.”

Not only did the plan help him set a personal best of 3:18:33 at Flying Pig, but it also helped him earn his Six Star Medal in New York and score a 2028 Boston Marathon qualifying time for his age group. Though he didn’t quite break 3:15 with his 3:21:27 performance, it marked his second-fastest marathon to date.

With a hectic schedule as a coach, Courtney Sobanski knew she needed a training plan that could fit into her everyday life. With our 3-Day training plan, Sobanski managed workouts successfully around other responsibilities—and remained injury-free. Our 3-Day plan features three key workouts a week—and any other days of easy running or cross-training you complete count as extra credit.

At the New York City Marathon, Sobanski crossed the finish line in 4:19:09 and told Runner’s World that she showed herself she could still run strong following foot surgery two years ago. “I’m just overcome with emotion that I actually did it and I can [run marathons] again,” Sobanski said following her race.

Ashley Osburn, 41, used the Break 4:30 plan to have every part of her training block mapped out in front of her—intervals, hills, tempo runs, long runs. Osburn said the plan made workouts approachable, and she appreciated the two weekly rest days built into the schedule for better recovery.

Though she didn’t quite reach her sub-4:30 goal in New York due to fueling missteps, Osburn intends to take another shot at the time barrier again in the future. “I will absolutely use [the training plan] again for my next marathon,” she said.

All of our Race With Runner’s World+ members had different goals and training plans pushing them toward the NYC finish line. But they all had a common shared experience of relishing the ecstatic crowds and infectious energy along the course through the five boroughs. “The crowd support all the way through was just amazing,” Dewalt said.

#8884. A 28-Year-Old Brooklyn Runner Died After Being Stabbed During an Evening Run. Police Are Still Searching for Her Attacker.

Katie Suarez’s death has left runners grieving and residents demanding better safety measures.

(Editor’s note: A 27-year-old man who worked for the city’s public school system was arrested and charged with the murder of Katie Suarez on Saturday, November 7, the New York Times reported.)

On Friday, October 30, Katie Suarez headed out at night along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway Greenway, a waterfront route she'd become quite familiar with from her regular runs around the neighborhood. The 28-year-old was stabbed in the neck that evening and died Monday, November 2, at NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn, her family confirmed.

The attack came just two days before the New York City Marathon, when the city was already buzzing with runners gearing up for Sunday's race. (Suarez was not registered for the event.) More than 60,000 people would be making their way through the five boroughs that weekend, but Suarez never got to finish her own run. Her death has since shaken the running community, particularly women who know all too well the safety concerns that can come with heading out alone.

Suarez usually met her parents after finishing up at the TD Bank near Caesar's Bay Shopping Center in Bath Beach where she worked, and joined them for the commute home. On the day of the attack, she switched into her running clothes and took off along the waterfront while her parents waited for her to return.

According to The New York Times, her father, Nery Suarez, called just before 8 p.m. to check on where she was. Katie told him she was only about half a mile away and would be back soon, but when more time passed without any sign of her, Nery and his wife, Yasira, became worried and went out looking for her.

Nery eventually found his daughter unconscious just off the running path near Bay 17th Street. She had suffered severe injuries to her neck and was rushed to the hospital, where she remained on life support until her death.

"I'm just left with this pain, and, oh my God, remembering my daughter as she was," Yasira told the New York Daily News on Tuesday. "She just wanted to run.”

As of November 6, police had not identified or arrested a suspect. NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said Monday that investigators were still trying to determine what led to the attack, though they had no reason to believe Suarez was specifically targeted and "right now, it seems that it's random.”

Finding evidence has been especially difficult along the section of the greenway where Suarez was attacked, which is dark and has no reported surveillance cameras. Investigators have searched the surrounding area using everything possible, from drones to police dogs and scuba divers, while also hoping passing motorists might have recorded something useful.

"We are looking for Teslas, we're looking for Uber drivers," Kenny said, explaining that dashcam footage could help police determine whether the attacker crossed the Belt Parkway while escaping.

The lack of lighting has also brought up plenty of concerns from people in the neighborhood who regularly use the path. At a vigil held Wednesday night, neighbors gathered near the waterfront to remember Suarez and discuss what needs to change to make the area safer after dark.

"There's no lights anywhere. It's very dark. A lot of trees, can't see anything," resident Ann Florio-Lopez told ABC7 New York.

Another woman at the vigil said she'd already changed her routine because of the attack, telling the station she “stopped walking at night.”

Runners outside Brooklyn have been speaking up as well, especially with the attack happening so close to marathon weekend. Fast Women shared Suarez's story on Instagram, expressing disappointment that her death hadn't received more attention within the running community. The account also pointed to complaints from locals who had reportedly been asking for better lighting and security along the greenway for years.

For Suarez's younger brother, Christopher, running has taken on a new meaning. He told 1010 WINS that Katie was always looking out for him, often calling to check in whenever he wasn't home at his usual time.

Now Christopher wants to honor her by running “all the miles she wanted to run” and the races she’ll never get the chance to do.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.
