#8834. Are These 5 Popular Running Recovery Strategies Hype or Legit?

The truth about cold plunging, saunas, foam rolling, and more.

Recovery is not the most exciting part of a runner’s training program—after all, it’s literally just the rest you take in between workouts—but ensuring high-quality recovery is essential if you want to maximize the gains of exercise and generally feel better after a butt-kicking run.

When good recovery is your goal, you’ll find no shortage of tools and strategies that promise to deliver exactly that—from cold plunges and saunas to foam rolling, compression gear, and more.

But as with many things in the wellness world, not everything that’s trendy is actually beneficial. So which recovery tactics are truly legit—and which ones are overhyped? We investigated five popular running recovery strategies to learn what’s worth your while… and what you could likely skip.

Recovery is when you give your body a break so that it can absorb the training you’re doing, Grace Horan, an exercise physiologist at the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS), tells Runner’s World.

There are four foundational elements to recovery, according to Horan: sleep, hydration, nutrition, and maintaining an appropriate training load (basically, keeping your easy runs easy and avoiding large spikes in training volume or intensity).

Other recovery tools can be used on top of that foundation—and we’ll dissect five of them in this article—but it’s important to first make sure that your foundation is solid, Horan says. In particular, sleep and nutrition are the most important, Horan says. If you aren’t locked in with those two, “all of the other recovery methods almost can go out the window,” Horan says.

Recovery is part of what Horan calls the “adaptation equation”: stress plus recovery equals adaptation.

Stress is all your training runs and workouts. Recovery includes the four foundational elements, along with any other recovery tools used on top of that. And adaptations are physiological changes that occur in response to training, such as improved endurance, increased aerobic capacity, and more strength and power in your muscles, Susan Kwiecen, PhD, principal scientist with the Gatorade Sports Science Institute and author of numerous publications on exercise recovery, tells Runner’s World.

Basically, you’re not getting stronger and more fit from training alone, but instead when you combine training with quality recovery.

These adaptations, says Kwiecen, are “ultimately what allow runners to become fitter and perform better over time.” And recovery—when done right—can enhance these adaptations by helping them happen better and faster. Recovery can also help you maintain performance by reducing soreness and managing fatigue, which allows you to run again as quickly as possible.

Keep in mind: “there’s no single best strategy for recovery,” Kwiecen says. “It depends really on the runner’s goals.”

Ah, the cold plunge. Most runners have a love-hate—or a straight-up hate-hate—relationship with this recovery tool. That’s because hanging out in frigid water is not very enjoyable in the moment. But is the discomfort worth it if your goal is recovery?

Possibly… with an asterisk. “The literature shows that cold plunges, ice baths, and cryotherapy in general can reduce soreness and help improve perceived recovery,” says Kwiecen. And if you feel less sore thanks to cold plunging, you may be able to perform better either that day or the next day. For that reason, cold plunges can be useful when your priority is rebounding between races or hard training sessions, Kwiecen says.

But here’s the catch: Regularly jumping in a cold plunge post training could reduce some of your fitness adaptations. Research shows this concern is most pronounced after resistance training, Kwiecen says. The cold temps can reduce blood flow to your muscles, which can decrease the opportunity for protein synthesis, ultimately blunting hypertrophy (muscle growth) and strength gains, Horan explains. Cold plunging may diminish endurance adaptations, too, Kwiecen adds.

So if you’re in a phase of training where your goal is to get stronger, “using cold plunges might not be the best idea,” Kwiecen says. Instead, they’d be better shelved for the end of a training block, when you’re no longer interested in gaining strength but simply want to feel as recovered as possible for your race.

Horan’s take: Cold plunges are not a recovery strategy that people should go out of their way to do, especially because the experience of cold plunging is “not super pleasant.” She personally doesn’t partake in cold plunging because “there are other recovery methods that are a little bit more gentle and a little less jarring that will have a very similar effect on perceived soreness and perceived recovery,” she explains.

That said, if you’re already an ice bath enthusiast, continuing the habit wouldn’t make or break your recovery or your training adaptations, Horan says.

If you do choose to cold plunge, pay attention to how your body reacts. Shivering, in particular, is a sign to end your session stat. “As soon as you start to shiver, you’re reversing all of the possible [recovery] benefits of cryotherapy,” Kwiecen explains.

Foam rolling can elicit a mixed bag of emotions from runners. Some athletes swear by their roller for reducing soreness and boosting mobility—and others try it and don’t feel any different, so they stop using it, Horan says.

Whatever camp you fall into, here’s the truth: “Rolling is definitely a low-risk option that can make runners feel looser and more prepared to train,” Kwiecen says. “It probably won’t ease muscle damage, but it can definitely help improve a runner’s mobility or comfort—both of which make it easier to complete planned training in the future.”

Horan personally loves foam rolling and does it after every run: “It’s low risk. It’s inexpensive. It does a few things reasonably well,” she says. That includes increasing range of motion and reducing feelings of soreness and general tightness after a run.

These benefits can be especially helpful for runners who are in an intense training block—for example, people nearing the end of marathon training. For some people, heavy training can really increase tightness in the fascia and muscles, Horan explains, in which case foam rolling can be an easy antidote.

Also cool: A foam rolling session doesn’t need to be long to be effective. “It’s something that you can get done in five minutes or less,” Horan says. She recommends runners focus their foam rolling on the quads, glutes, calves, and hamstrings (though she adds that stretching the hamstrings is potentially more effective than foam rolling them). Spend about 30 seconds to 1 minute per side of each muscle group, she advises.

For each muscle group, roll up and down the big muscle belly (rather than near the tendons) and pause when you find a spot that feels super tight, Horan says. From there, contract the muscle you’re foam rolling, which helps the foam rolling penetrate deeper into the myofascia, she explains. For example, kick your heel to your butt multiple times to contract the quad, or point and flex your foot to contract your calves.

Many runners foam roll after their workouts. But it can also be a helpful tool in your warmups to help you feel loose and move efficiently during a long run or race, Kwiecen says.

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—which you can find over-the-counter as Advil, Motrin, Aleve, or Aspirin—are a type of medication that some runners take to ward off post-exercise discomfort.

The purpose of these drugs is to reduce pain and inflammation, Kwiecen says. And that can be helpful… when there is a valid medical reason, Horan says. But Kwiecen and Horan agree NSAIDs shouldn’t be a routine recovery strategy from running—a stance supported by other experts and research.

Part of that is because the stress of training triggers an inflammatory response in most people, Horan says. That might sound bad, but it’s actually a good thing: This specific type of inflammation is a normal, natural reaction to exercise that “needs to take place for us to adapt optimally to the stress that we’re giving our body,” Horan explains. Taking NSAIDs suppresses that inflammatory response, which can ultimately minimize our gains from training, she explains.

Plus, taking NSAIDs to mitigate pain you’re feeling from running can cause you to continue training through an issue that would be better solved with rest, training modification, and potentially getting evaluated by a medical provider, Kwiecen points out. “Reducing pain and improving recovery are not the same thing,” she says.

Bottom line: Runners shouldn’t rely on NSAIDs as a recovery strategy. If you’re an athlete who thinks you need this medication for another reason, Horan recommends consulting with your doctor on the pros and cons.

Compression garments—in the form of socks, pants, and pneumatic compression boots—are a popular choice for runners looking to accelerate their recovery after long or hard runs. But do they work?

This is another recovery strategy that does have legit benefits… but also comes with an asterisk. Horan generally likes compression garments, saying they can help boost a runner’s comfort, perceived recovery, and blood flow post exercise. Research also shows that using compression gear can help you feel less sore, Kwiecen adds. But here’s a caveat: You need a certain level of compression in order to achieve that reduction in soreness—and it can be difficult to get that from commercially available products, Kwiecen says. As she puts it: “Compression garments are tricky.”

That said, they’re a pretty low-risk strategy, meaning they likely won’t harm your recovery in any way, Horan says. “There are people that will wear their pneumatic compression boots after every single run, and if they love it, then I think that’s great,” she says. At the same time, some compression garments—particularly the pneumatic boots—can be pricey, and by no means are they essential to a quality recovery. As Horan puts it: “I don’t think people need to go out and buy $500 boots if it’s not something that they already love.”

Unlike cold plunges or tight compression gear, saunas are one of those recovery strategies that feel good in the moment (and often afterward, too). “People love a sauna—myself included,” says Horan. They can help usher in a sense of relaxation and may also reduce feelings of soreness, Horan says.

Beyond those recovery benefits, saunas could also help stimulate adaptations that benefit endurance performance, Kwiecen adds. More specifically, sauna sessions count as heat exposure, which spurs the production of heat shock proteins, Kwiecen explains. “These proteins protect and repair cells when they’re under stress,” she says. This means sauna sessions can help the body adapt to heat, “which can be beneficial when preparing for races in warm conditions,” Kwiecen says. Horan agrees that sauna sessions can help runners acclimate to heat if used regularly.

That said, saunas do have their limitations: They aren’t going to erase muscle damage or speed up recovery, Kwiecen says. Even so, Horan sees them as a “great” option for runners who enjoy them and have the time for them in their schedule.

Just be careful about jumping into a sauna immediately following a long run, especially if you’re already dehydrated, Horan says. That’s because you’ll likely sweat in the sauna, which will cause you to become even more dehydrated. And proper hydration, like we mentioned, is an essential component to good recovery.

Also, for general safety, don’t spend a ton of concentrated time in the sauna. Unlike the cold plunge, there’s no reverse shivering response for the sauna, Kwiecen says. As a general rule of thumb, though, cap your sessions at 10 to 12 minutes (or get out sooner if you start feeling unwell). As long as you follow these general guidelines, “if you’re well-hydrated and you really like to be in a sauna, I say go for it,” Horan says.

Runners should steer clear of using NSAIDs as a routine recovery tool, in part, because they can blunt fitness adaptations and cause runners to train through pain, which can increase injury risk. As for the other four strategies mentioned here—cold plunges, saunas, foam rolling, and compression gear—Kwiecen’s stance is that “if it makes you feel better, go for it.” That’s because when you feel better, chances are you’ll perform better the next time you go out for a run. “It’s all super subjective,” Kwiecen says, adding that not many recovery modalities have strong science-backed benefits beyond the feeling of less soreness.

Also keep in mind: The “right” recovery strategy may change throughout your training cycle and overall running journey. “Matching the recovery strategy to the runner’s goal is important,” Kwiecen says. For example, because cold plunging can blunt strength gains, it may not be the best choice when your goal is to get stronger—but perhaps it does have a time and place right before a big race, when your main priority is minimizing soreness.

Whichever recovery strategies you choose to use, remember to first prioritize the fundamentals. “Nothing,” says Horan, “will ever, ever, ever beat sleeping enough, eating enough, drinking enough water, and avoiding really sharp spikes in intensity or volume load.”

Jenny is a Boulder, Colorado-based health and fitness journalist. She’s been freelancing for Runner’s World since 2015 and especially loves to write human interest profiles, in-depth service pieces and stories that explore the intersection of exercise and mental health. Her work has also been published by SELF, Men’s Journal, and Condé Nast Traveler, among other outlets. When she’s not running or writing, Jenny enjoys coaching youth swimming, rereading Harry Potter, and buying too many houseplants.

#8831. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis)

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

For Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

“I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the big mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

“I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

“I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

“If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the big training blocks start.”

Head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’

“I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

“For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the new technique as you can sustain, and no more.

“You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

“For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”

“A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most important session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”

#8830. Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

Lab safety scores matter, but so do fit, ventilation, and price. Here’s how the top lids compare.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

So, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

“The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

In our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8829. The 8 Best Altra Running Shoes for Runners Who Hate Cramped Toes and Want to Try Zero-Drop

Altra is known for its women-specific fit, wide toebox, and zero-drop cushioning. We recommend the best Altra shoes—including those with a 4mm offset—out now.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 10, 2026: Need some support trying low drop? The Altra Experience Form is now 24% off—but inventory is low, so stock up now!

Altra holds a special place in my heart because one of the first shoes I reviewed after I was hired at Runner’s World was the brand’s now-discontinued Instinct/Intuition 4.5. Altra was founded in 2009 by high school running buddies Golden Harper and Brian Beckstead. Turns out the Instinct/Intuition was pivotal to Altra establishing itself in the running industry. It was the first model Altra launched in 2011.

Since my introduction to Altra, I’ve witnessed its evolution; the brand formerly known for strictly selling zero-drop shoes (when forefoot and heel cushioning are equal) has added models with a 4mm drop. This move has drawn the zero-drop-curious to the Altra way.

Looking for a zero-drop daily trainer → Altra Torin 9 (Men’s/Women’s)

In need of stability → Altra Experience Form (Men’s/Women’s)

Curious to try low-drop → Altra Experience Flow 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Shopping for a low-drop trail shoe → Altra Experience Wild 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Racing a marathon → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Logging long runs → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s)

Wanting a true racing flat → Altra Escalante 5 (Men’s/Women’s)

A lover of gnarly trails → Altra Lone Peak 9+ (Men’s/Women’s)

Balanced Cushioning, which refers to the shoe’s heel-to-toe drop, or lack thereof. Altra designs most of its shoes with no drop, meaning your foot sits flat rather than sloping downward from heel to toe. According to Altra, this can help promote your natural stride and encourage a lower-impact landing—because the heel isn’t as beefed up, you’re less likely to land on it.

Altra also introduced its 4mm line of shoes so runners can ease into zero-drop with an offset that’s approximately two stacked nickels.

The first time I ran in Altras, I couldn’t help feeling like I was wearing clown shoes. Unbox a pair of Altras and you’ll see that the forefoot is much wider than on other shoes; the enlarged, anatomical toe box allows the foot to expand and gives the toes room to splay. Altra now has three different foot shapes: original (the widest), standard, and slim (the narrowest).

Wide-foot runners and runners with bunions appreciate the roominess in the toe area. But all runners can benefit from wearing Altra’s foot-shaped trainers. A narrow toebox that cramps your toes can negatively affect your performance (and set you up for injuries).

The company uses three main cushioning materials in its shoes: Ego, Ego Max, and Ego Pro.

Ego: Compared to traditional EVA, this foam provides a springier feel and more durability.

Ego Max: A foam made of compression-molded EVA and tuned for a softer feel than Ego, but it isn’t as responsive.

Ego Pro: Altra’s top-shelf foam made of thermoplastic elastomers (TPE) formed in a supercritical fluid process. It’s the brand’s lightest and most responsive cushioning material.

P35X: Altra’s new and improved version of Ego foam that’s lighter and more efficient.

Altra’s stability tech is its guide rail, which is a layer of dense midsole foam that is raised on the medial side. The guide rail serves as a “bumper” that helps counter overpronation during your stride.

Altra’s women’s shoes are built on a women’s-specific last to match the biomechanics of female feet. These shoes are narrower through the heel and midfoot and better accommodate women’s generally longer arches.

Since my introduction to Altra as a new hire at Runner’s World in 2018, I have tested several models by the brand, appreciating the shoes’ generous toe room on my wide feet. I have tested all of the shoes in this buying guide and delved into the feedback of our 350-plus shoe testers. These local runners present an inclusive testing pool, ranging in gait patterns, arch heights, and experience levels.

*All weights are for men’s 10 and women’s 8.

The Torin has undergone a revamp with its ninth iteration—but rest assured, all these changes are welcomed upgrades.

The shoe has a new Vibram outsole, which inspired our testers to take the shoe off the road and onto the trail. “I felt that the shoe performed best on a packed dirt/trail surface where it felt like it had a great traction and springy push off. Those trail runs were at a 7:00 to 7:30 pace,” said tester Steven Blasi.

On the road and off, the Torin 9 is bouncier and softer too. Altra’s P35X midsole makes for a more cushioned ride without silencing ground feel. The support makes the shoe a great entry into zero-drop for newbies.

Lastly, the fit is more accommodating. The non-gusseted tongue provides a roomier fit for those with high insteps.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Experience Form provides stability when you need it with Altra’s guide rail. Acting as a “bumper” on the medial side, the feature lends support to overpronators and neutral runners, alike.

“I liked the overall stability and comfort of the shoe,” said Anthony Dentino, a heel-striker who runs with a neutral gait. “The shoe was firm but provided excellent cushioning throughout, especially in the heel. Because of its weight, this is not a shoe that I would suggest for speedwork or racing but it is an excellent training shoe.”

Another favorite feature was the shoe’s hardiness and trustworthiness in inclement weather.

“I wore them multiple times in the rain and on some snowy surfaces, but felt like they provided good traction every time,” said overpronator Alyssa Dever. “Not only that, they did not soak through easily in the rain, and kept my feet warm in cold temperatures (some sub-20-degree runs).”

Shop Men’s at rei.com Shop Women’s at rei.com

If switching to zero-drop still sounds like taking a major leap, you can opt for running in the Experience Flow 3 before you go for a spin in the Torin 8. The Experience Flow has a 4mm offset, which is approximately the same depth of two nickels stacked on top of each other. The heel lift is subtle, allowing you to ease into running in a low-drop shoe.

Testers loved the versatility of the shoe, appreciating its supportive Altra Ego midsole. For some, it hit that Goldilocks sweet spot of feeling not too firm, nor too soft.

“I loved that it was a not a minimalist shoe, but wasn’t the huge cloud cushion kind either,” said tester Chris Greg. “It was a happy medium between the two where I felt connected to the ground but was offered plenty of support to make my 5-mile runs smooth.”

Others described the cushioning as having just the right amount of “squishiness.”

“I really loved how much cushioning these shoes had,” said tester Mary Hartnett. “It made my runs feel so much easier and ‘squishier’ compared to other shoes I’ve used. This extra softness was a huge help during my training because I actually felt excited to put them on every morning, and my feet didn’t feel as tired afterward.”

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

We’ve loved the Experience Wild since its first iteration. The shoe is outfitted for technical trails, offering protection with a toe sweep, gaiter attachment points, and a grippy MaxTrac outsole that can handle loose, uneven terrain. It’s also a great option for those who run on bridle paths and groomed rail trails. The Experience Wild 3 is flexible, has an accommodating wide fit in the midfoot and toe area, and a padded tongue that makes the fit snug and enclosed, so pebbles and sand can be kept out.

The biggest update to the Experience Wild 3 is the mesh upper, which provides a more secure fit and more breathability.

“V3 takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, a more plush cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remaining stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” said tester John Mikovits.

The Experience Wild 3+ ($165) is also available and has a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Vanish Carbon 3 feels like a true super while preserving Altra’s fit and feel. The racing shoe is the first in its line with a 4mm offset; the Altra shoe team realized their super shoe needed a drop so they wouldn’t be outmatched by competitors. Altra’s running economy tests showed the Vanish Carbon 3 had 2.6 percent better running economy compared to the Vanish Carbon 2.

A carbon plate is sandwiched between FastRce, which is pure PEBA. The plate has a split big toe to allow for engagement and power. All this is housed in an upper with Altra’s signature roomy toebox that provides generous wiggle room for your toes to splay.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

As of updating this buying guide, I only just laced up in the Fwd Via 2 after meeting with Altra at the Runner’s World Shoe Summit before the NYC Marathon. The original Fwd Via was an instant favorite from first run. The shoe has a rocker profile and high cushioning, making the low heel-to-toe drop easier to get used to if you’re a zero-drop virgin. It’s great for long runs and recovery runs, and has a generous bed of foam for run/walkers.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

It’s been two and a half years since the release of the Escalante 4—but the Escalante 5 makes that length of time worth the wait.

Nothing has dramatically changed with the Escalante 5: same roomy toebox, same breathable knit upper, same Ego midsole, and same 24 mm stack height. Instead of fully revamping the shoe, the Altra team refined it with a few tweaks.

The strobel and sockliner are made of TPEE for even more comfort. In this way, you still get plenty of ground feel in this minimalistic, lightweight trainer, but with added comfort and support. The outsole also has more rubber to enhance traction and durability.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Lone Peak 9+ is the first iteration of the shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole. This makes the shoe have outstanding traction on wet or dry surfaces. RW Tester feedback confirms Vibram Megagrip’s traction on uneven, slippery terrain.

Said tester Shelby Brett, “I greatly appreciate that the lugs on the shoe are significant and that they go in multiple directions, again adding to my confidence underfoot.”

The shoe has a durable ripstop upper and an extra eyelet for a more locked-in fit. Testers loved the ground feel of the Lone Peak 9+, saying the shoe had the perfect balance of cushioning and protection. Another highlight was that spacious toebox.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

We recommend starting slow and short if it’s your first time running in zero-drop shoes. Shoes with a drop have more cushioning in the heel. If you’re a heel-striker, you may need to run in a zero-drop shoe with a higher stack height to provide more support under the heel area. Try Altra’s 4mm shoes first to become accustomed to a lower-drop shoe.

What is the difference between Altra’s guide rail and Brooks’s guide rails?

Altra’s guide rail runs along the medial side of the shoe, acting as a bumper and preventing your foot from collapsing during sharp turns or if your feet roll inward during your gait cycle (overpronation).

Brooks’s guide rails are on the medial and lateral sides of the shoe. Like Altra’s guide rail, the guide rails also provide stability when you need it, making the shoes supportive for overpronators and neutral runners. The guide rails act as bumpers, helping align the knee and ankle.

#8828. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

Your power meter might be working perfectly, but that doesn’t mean your cycling computer records data accurately. Here’s why you should care and how you can check.

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The big problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

The same seat — Washington Dulles to Doha, with the ability to continue to dozens of destinations across Asia, Africa, and beyond — retails for **$5,000 to $9,000 in cash**. At 70,000 AAdvantage miles, you're extracting between **7.1 and 12.9 cents per point**. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This redemption is *three to six times that*. This is what the FI community means when we talk about travel rewards as a genuine wealth multiplier. If you've been stockpiling points wondering whether they're actually worth something, this is your answer. A cash ticket that costs more than many people's monthly take-home salary becomes nearly free with the right points strategy. The inefficiency exists because AAdvantage still prices partner awards — flights on airlines like Qatar, JAL, and Cathay Pacific — on a **fixed partner award chart** rather than the dynamic pricing it uses for American-operated flights. Qatar, as a oneworld alliance member, is required to make award space available to partner programs. American prices that space at a flat 70,000 miles for business class, regardless of what Qatar itself charges in cash or its own Avios currency. The result is a structural arbitrage opportunity: you're using a fixed-price chart to book a premium product that Qatar prices at whatever the market will bear — and the market bears a *lot* for QSuites. The ChooseFI community has long understood that the highest-leverage use of points isn't domestic economy upgrades. It's premium international cabin redemptions where the gap between cash price and points cost is widest. On that spectrum, QSuites via AAdvantage sits near the very top.

The core insight here is understanding two separate pricing systems operating simultaneously. Qatar Airways prices its QSuites cabin dynamically in cash — demand surges around holidays, business travel seasons, and major events can push that $5,000 base price to $9,000 or beyond. But American AAdvantage doesn't care about any of that. As a oneworld alliance partner, AAdvantage uses a fixed partner award chart for Qatar redemptions: 70,000 miles one-way in business class, full stop.

This means the more expensive the cash ticket gets, the better your CPP becomes — without you doing anything differently. Book during peak travel periods when cash prices spike to $9,000, and you're extracting 12.9 cents per AAdvantage mile. Even at the floor — a $5,000 cash ticket — you're at 7.1 cents per point. AAdvantage periodically runs "Web Specials" — discounted partner awards where pricing drops significantly below the standard chart. These specials are unpredictable and availability is limited, but if you're flexible on travel dates, checking AA.com regularly for Web Specials on Qatar routes can yield an even better deal.

ChooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

Let's run the numbers on a concrete example.

The Route: Washington Dulles (IAD) to Doha (DOH) on Qatar Airways QR 22, operating a Boeing 777-300ER with QSuites. This is a nonstop flight of approximately 13 hours — exactly the kind of long-haul journey where your seat product matters enormously.

The Cash Price: A business class ticket on this route typically runs $5,500 to $7,500, and during peak travel windows — think spring break, summer, or major holidays — it can reach $9,000. Call it a realistic average of $6,500.

The Points Cost: 70,000 AAdvantage miles + approximately $80–$120 in taxes and fees.

The Math: At $6,500 cash value against 70,000 miles, you're getting 9.3 cents per point. Against a $9,000 peak ticket, you're at 12.9 cents per point. Either way, this is among the highest-value AAdvantage redemptions available anywhere in the program.

You arrive at Dulles and proceed to the Qatar Airways check-in counter, where you're processed as a business class passenger. At Doha, you'll have access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world, featuring a full à la carte restaurant, shower suites, and a calm, spacious environment that makes a layover feel genuinely pleasant.

Onboard, your QSuite is a private cabin with a door that slides closed. The bed extends to a full 80 inches. You'll be offered a genuine dine-on-demand service — no scheduled meal times, no "chicken or pasta" announcements over the intercom. The wine list is serious. The bedding is from The White Company. The 21.5-inch screen is 4K.

For the ChooseFI community, the most powerful part of this isn't the luxury itself — it's the ratio. You're experiencing a $6,500–$9,000 product for the cost of points you earned on everyday spending and a small tax outlay. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: maximum experience per dollar (or point) deployed.

Do this: Book as far out as possible. AAdvantage allows bookings up to 331 days in advance. Qatar releases its best award inventory to partner programs at the time of schedule opening — not closer to departure. If you have a target travel window, search at the 331-day mark. Availability genuinely deteriorates as departure approaches.

Do this: Watch for Web Special pricing drops. AAdvantage's Web Specials have historically offered Qatar business class awards at 50,000 miles instead of the standard 70,000. These appear without warning on aa.com under the "Web Specials" tab. If you're flexible with your dates within a week or two, checking this section regularly (or signing up for AAdvantage email alerts) can save you 20,000 miles — a meaningful difference.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou for same-day transfers. If you find award space and need to transfer points immediately, Citi ThankYou → AAdvantage transfers are instant. This is the fastest transfer path and eliminates the risk of space disappearing while your transfer processes. Keep Citi points in reserve as your QSuites "strike fund."

Avoid this: Transferring Marriott points unless absolutely necessary. The Marriott Bonvoy → AAdvantage transfer at 3:1 is deeply inefficient. You're spending three Marriott points to create one AAdvantage mile. Marriott points are worth roughly 0.7–0.8 cents each, meaning you're paying effectively 2.1–2.4 cents per AAdvantage mile — still potentially worth it for QSuites, but exhaust your Citi and Bilt options first.

Do this: Treat DOH as a hub, not a destination. Doha is Qatar's base, meaning a 70,000-mile award from the US to DOH can be the first leg of an onward journey to destinations across Asia, South Asia, or East Africa — all on Qatar metal. A trip from IAD to Singapore (SIN) routing through DOH, for example, puts you in QSuites for the transatlantic leg and potentially a narrowbody for the shorter DOH-SIN segment.

Avoid this: Booking round-trip when one-way is more flexible. AAdvantage allows one-way partner awards. Book your outbound and return separately — this dramatically expands your availability options and lets you mix partners or return on a different airline without being locked into a single itinerary.

Do this: Build AAdvantage miles through Bilt's monthly rent payments. Bilt Rewards is the only major program that earns points on rent. If you're paying $1,500–$2,500/month in rent, a year of Bilt earning generates 18,000–30,000 Bilt points — transferable to AAdvantage at 1:1. That's a meaningful contribution to your 70,000-mile target from a spend category you have anyway.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is purpose-built for the serious couple or solo traveler with a specific long-haul itinerary in mind — a honeymoon, a milestone anniversary trip, a once-in-a-while splurge that you've decided to fund with points rather than cash. If your travel goal is experiencing a world-class business class product nearly free, this is among the best vehicles in the entire points ecosystem.

Minimum requirements: 70,000 AAdvantage miles per person, plus $80–$150 in cash for taxes and fees. You also need the patience and flexibility to find saver award space, which is the primary friction in this redemption.

## Honest Difficulty Assessment: Moderate This redemption scores **moderate difficulty** — and that rating is accurate. It's not a click-and-book process like domestic awards, but it's not the multi-step puzzle that some ultra-premium redemptions require either. The difficulty is concentrated in **two specific areas**. **Challenge #1: Finding Available Award Space** Qatar releases QSuites award inventory to AAdvantage, but not generously. Availability scores a **2 out of 5**, which means you will sometimes search for weeks before finding the right date. This is the primary bottleneck. The fix: search early (331 days out), be flexible within a 1-2 week window, and use ExpertFlyer alerts to get notified when space opens. Midweek departures and shoulder-season travel windows (late January through March, September through November) tend to surface more space. **Challenge #2: Building 70,000 AAdvantage Miles** AAdvantage's transfer partner list is narrower than Chase or Amex ecosystems. Your best paths are Citi ThankYou (instant transfers) and Bilt Rewards (1-2 days). This earns a **3 out of 5** for ease of earning — achievable, but requires intentional card strategy rather than casual accumulation. **The booking process itself** — once you have miles and availability — is straightforward on aa.com. AAdvantage's award search tool clearly displays partner availability and pricing. **The encouragement:** Every traveler in the ChooseFI community who has navigated this redemption consistently describes it as worth every minute of the search process. The moment that QSuite door closes, you'll understand exactly why. If you're willing to invest the time to find availability and build your miles intentionally, this redemption is entirely within reach — and the payoff is extraordinary.

Log into your AAdvantage account and search for one-way business class flights on your desired route. Filter for partner-operated flights and look specifically for Qatar Airways (QR) flight numbers. The search results will show the mileage cost alongside availability.

If aa.com does not show availability, search the same route on Qatar's own website using a Privilege Club account. Qatar sometimes releases space that AA's system takes 24-48 hours to reflect. If you find space on Qatar but not AA, check back the following day.

Not all Qatar business class flights operate QSuites. Check the aircraft type listed in the search results — A350-1000 and select 777-300ERs have QSuites. Verify on SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to ensure you are booking the premium product.

Once you confirm QSuites availability, complete the booking on aa.com using your AAdvantage miles. The process is the same as booking any AA award flight. You will see the mileage cost plus taxes and fees before confirming.

American Airlines charges approximately 70,000 AAdvantage miles one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights. Taxes and fees are typically $30 to $80. A round trip comes to roughly 140,000 miles total plus minimal fees.

Both options cost roughly 70,000 points one-way. The main differences are earning sources and booking experience. AAdvantage miles are earned through Citi cards and Bilt, while Avios can be earned through Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. AA offers web booking while BA may require phone calls. Check availability through both programs — they sometimes see different award space.

Yes. The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select earns bonus miles on purchases, Bilt Rewards transfers to AAdvantage at 1:1, AA's SimplyMiles program earns miles on everyday purchases linked to your credit card, and the AAdvantage shopping portal earns miles at online retailers. You can accumulate 70,000 or more miles without taking a single AA flight.

Airlines control how much award inventory they release to each partner. Qatar may release seats to BA's Avios program but not to AA, or vice versa. AA's search engine also has known inconsistencies with partner availability display. Always cross-reference qatarairways.com and ba.com if aa.com shows no availability on your desired dates.

Using AAdvantage miles for Qatar business class is one of the strongest partner award redemptions in the oneworld alliance. At 70,000 miles for a product that retails at $5,000 to $8,000, the value per mile is outstanding. The web-based booking experience on aa.com removes the friction of phone calls, and the lack of fuel surcharges keeps your cash outlay minimal. If you earn AAdvantage miles through Citi cards or Bilt transfers, this should be at the top of your aspirational redemption list. Search early, stay flexible on dates, and book the moment QSuites space appears.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Many of us started running in a Brooks trainer, and with Black Friday deals in full swing, you can stock up on must-have Brooks gear or gift that friend you’re pushing to run their first 5K.

What makes Brooks trainers so popular? Their plush, slipper-like fit and comfy cushioning put them at the center of a Venn diagram where dad shoes and serious runner trainers converge.

Several top-rated models, like the Adrenaline GTS 25, are on sale at brooksrunning.com and sites like REI and Amazon. But sizes and colors are limited, so stock up now before they’re gone for good!

We’ve also included discounted Brooks apparel, so you can run in Brooks from head to toe all winter long.

Brooks Running Sale | REI Brooks Running Sale

The stability counterpart to the Ghost 18, the Adrenaline GTS is the shoe many of us ran in when we fell in love with running. The 25th iteration is the lightest yet, with a foamy midsole, the brand’s DNA Loft v3, to absorb shock and provide soft landings. The guide rails system is Brooks’s unobtrusive stability tech for neutral runners and overpronators alike. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides acts as bumpers to help align your knee and ankle.

“This is a fantastic shoe,” said tester Chris Garges, an overpronator and heel striker. “I’ve run in every model Adrenaline dating back to the Adrenaline 3, and this is by far the best shoe in the series. I loved everything from the fit to the ride to the cushioning.”

Brooks wanted to change what we should expect when running in a max-cushioned trainer. “We noticed that for some people, they would start running in a neutral shoe and then their body would work extra. So the internal cost was actually increasing,” said Brooks Footwear PLM and BlueLine Director Nikhil Jain.

The team set out to create a shoe that would cut that internal cost. The Glycerin Flex has a decoupled heel and Flex Zone; these components allow your foot to flex naturally instead of working against a stiff, beefy platform.

“Testing the Brooks Glycerin Flex was a novel experience for me on multiple fronts,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Not only was this the first Brooks running shoe I’ve ever run in, but it was also the first hyperflexible shoe that I have ever seen—and overall, it was a positive experience. The Glycerin Flex combines the benefits of a daily trainer that allows your feet to work and get stronger with the comfort and protection of a maximalist shoe.”

We like the Glycerin Max 2 for run/walking and recovery days. The shoe has 45 mm of DNA Tuned foam in the heel and a 6 mm offset. Its beefiness was off-putting for some, especially for runners hoping to get in some tempo work on their long runs. But testers said the cushioning was extremely comfy on slow days.

“I loved how comfortable the sneaker was. I instantly felt supported and it felt like I was walking on a bouncy pillow,” said wear-tester Steph Norman. “This sneaker would be great for easy/long miles where you do not have to worry about your feet hurting.”

The popular Brooks Ghost hits the trails. The shoe is outfitted for going off-road with 3 mm lugs on the TrailTack rubber outsole.

Our tester, David Hinkl, appreciated how the shoe protected his feet on gnarly surfaces. “The best part of the shoe for me was the sole,” he said. “It was beefy enough to prevent sharp rocks and pointy things from getting to my feet. Training is more fun when I don’t have to tiptoe across the trail.”

The Canopy is iconic. Despite the curtains of rain, monstrous winds, and cold temps, Des Linden was the first American woman to win the 2018 Boston Marathon after 33 years. And she wore the Canopy Jacket. This version of the Canopy (the original is also on sale with 30 percent off) can be packed into a little pouch that’s easy to store in the depths of an overpacked duffel.

The High Point keeps out the rain without overheating. Venting in the back allows airflow, while waterproof fabric and sealed inner seams keep you from getting soaked during a downpour. The jacket also packs down into a pocket.

These joggers are the softest joggers we’ve tested. They’re great for warmups, cooldowns, and traveling. I should know—I trekked Japan after running the Tokyo Marathon in these.

The Run Visible not only ensures you’re seen with reflective detail, but it also keeps you warm thanks to Thermolite insulation. Three pockets provide storage. That hi-vis orange color also helps you pop out in low light.

The Chaser is for runners who love a soft compression short with ample storage. The high-rise Chaser has side pockets for stashing your phone and leg-opening grippers to prevent them from riding up.

#8825. You Don’t Need a Weight Room to Build Cycling Power—You Just Need This One Compact Piece of Equipment

Build core strength, stability, and mobility at home with one compact training tool.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

If a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

One of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training plans, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

One great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

If you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

You can find our complete expert-recommended workout here. The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
